fields.description:
Franklin Roosevelt enters the 1940 campaign as the two term incumbent, and already one of the most consequential Presidents in American history. During his first 4 years in office, Roosevelt passed an expansive list of social and economic programs, giving him great popularity across the nation, and allowing his historic reelection victory in 1936.

But with the political headwinds of his second term -- popular opposition to his court packing scheme, attempts to purge his own party in 1938, and recession -- along with the outbreak of war in Europe, have put it in serious doubt that Roosevelt can become the first President in history to win a third term.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1940 election.

The two-term tradition is broken, and you have four more years. Don't celebrate too much, however. The debate over how far to go in aiding Britain is far from settled, and the draft is already proving controversial. Domestically, the tensions between organized labor and the southern wing of your party are only going to get worse. Good luck!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1940 election.

It seems the controversies of court packing, the recession of '37, and your attempted purge of conservative Democrats all came home to roost. Regardless, you leave office with a record of domestic achievement that will be debated for generations. Willkie has promised not to dismantle the New Deal, but he will be under enormous pressure from his own party to do exactly that.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! It's headed to Congress!

The Electoral College has failed to produce a winner. The contest goes to the House, where the southern Democrats will likely decide things. They are still furious about the purge attempt in '38, and they are not inclined to do you any favors. Good luck!

fields.description:
Wendell Willkie, a businessman, has shocked the political establishment by successfully leaving the Republican National Convention as his party’s nominee -- despite only having joined it less than half a year ago. He is a hardline internationalist and liberal who secured the nomination with major media support, often putting him at odds with Republican leadership, who believe he shares more with Roosevelt politically than he does with them.

Faced with the tough task of challenging an incumbent President, Willkie must unite the Republican Party’s conservative and liberal wings, while pressing Roosevelt on the third term issue if he is to win this election.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1940 election.

Congratulations! You have defeated Franklin Roosevelt and ended the third term before it started. Nobody saw this coming when you walked into the Republican convention four months ago. Your first order of business will be the crisis in Europe. Churchill is desperate for American aid, and Congress will be watching closely to see how far you go. The New Deal programs are likely here to stay in some form, whatever congressional Republicans might prefer. Good luck!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1940 election.

Ultimately, the power of incumbency and the war scare in Europe were just a little too much to overcome. You ran a strong campaign for a man with no political experience, and you've established yourself as a figure of real national prominence. What will you do now? You could run for senate, complete your take-over of the Republican party, or simply promote your ideals as a private citizen. Good luck!
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! It's headed to Congress!

No candidate has won a majority in the Electoral College, and the contest moves to the House of Representatives. The southern Democrats hold the balance of power, and they have grievances with Roosevelt going back to the court packing fight and the '38 purge. Whether they are willing to hand the presidency to a Republican to settle those scores remains to be seen. Good luck!

fields.description_as_running_mate:
Henry Wallace is the current Secretary of Agriculture and one of the chief architects of the New Deal's agricultural programs, winning loyalty from farmers across the Midwest and South through the Agricultural Adjustment Act. His home state of Iowa and neighboring farm states could be meaningfully shored up by his presence on the ticket.

Wallace has little political base beyond his bureaucratic accomplishments, and conservatives within the party find him too liberal for comfort -- though he is unlikely to cost Roosevelt any states he would otherwise carry.

William Bankhead is the powerful Speaker of the House and one of the most respected figures in the Democratic Party. His selection would soothe Southern conservatives grown restless under Roosevelt's second term, shoring up the Solid South at a moment when the New Deal has strained those loyalties.

However, Bankhead is in poor health, and his association with the party's conservative wing may dampen enthusiasm among the labor and progressive voters Roosevelt will need to turn out in large numbers to win an unprecedented third term.

Paul McNutt is the former Governor of Indiana and current High Commissioner to the Philippines. A serious presidential contender in his own right, his loyalty to the ticket is something of an open question. He is handsome, charismatic, and broadly popular, and Indiana would be a meaningful pickup. However, he is closely associated with the interventionist American Legion and has attracted some criticism for what opponents describe as an authoritarian governing style as Indiana's governor.

His support for social security expansion has made him popular with labor, but he has never built a strong ideological identity that would excite any particular wing of the party.

Jesse Jones is the powerful overseer of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, a Texas businessman who has won the confidence of both Wall Street and Main Street -- a rare feat in the Roosevelt years. His selection would reassure conservatives grown wary of the New Deal, and Texas is a state Roosevelt will want firmly in his column.

Jones has frequently clashed with the administration's more liberal impulses, and his selection would be read by labor and progressives as a signal that Roosevelt is tacking right. He is also more of a boardroom figure than a campaigner, and it is not clear he has the political instincts or the appetite for the rough and tumble of a national campaign.

Charles McNary is the Senate Minority Leader from Oregon and the natural choice for a party looking to balance its ticket. Two decades in the Senate have made him a well-regarded institutionalist on both sides of the aisle, and his long advocacy for farm relief gives him appeal in the rural West, a useful counterweight to a Wall Street utility executive with no prior political experience.

However, McNary has been a consistent supporter of the public power projects that Willkie built his career fighting against, creating an awkward ideological tension at the top of the ticket. He is also in declining health, and brings little excitement to a party already gambling heavily on the unconventional Willkie as its standard bearer.

Arthur Vandenberg is the senior Senator from Michigan and one of the party's most respected figures, a serious nomination contender whose selection would help heal a convention that steamrolled the party establishment. His expertise on foreign affairs would provide institutional credibility to a ticket headed by a political newcomer.

However, Vandenberg is a committed isolationist at a moment when Willkie has broken sharply from the party mainstream by openly sympathizing with Britain. His cool relationship with Willkie and thwarted presidential ambitions may also make him a reluctant partner on the trail.

John Bricker is the Governor of Ohio and a stalwart of the party's conservative, isolationist wing. His selection would reassure Republicans uncomfortable with Willkie's interventionism and recent conversion from the Democrats, and his solid midwestern conservatism provides a sharp contrast to Willkie's freewheeling Wall Street persona.

However, the very qualities that make him appealing to the party base are liabilities in a general election. His hard isolationism will look increasingly untenable as Europe's crisis deepens, and his conventional party regularity does little to reinforce Willkie's argument that he represents something fresh in American politics.

Raymond Baldwin is the recently elected Governor of Connecticut, a liberal internationalist and one of Willkie's most prominent convention backers -- indeed his own preferred choice for the vice presidency. His progressive Yankee Republicanism is well suited to appealing to the urban voters Willkie will need to peel away from Roosevelt.

He is, however, a relatively obscure figure nationally, and brings little institutional heft to a ticket that might benefit from a running mate who can reassure voters there are steady hands somewhere on board.

fields.description:
Left for dead politically, President Bill Clinton has a tough road ahead to re-election. He’s dealt with foreign policy crises, unpopular budgets, and a growing set of scandals. But with an intractable Republican Congress led by firebrand Newt Gingrich, the President’s best bet to win a second term may be painting his opponents as obstructionists halting the nation’s progress.

But Clinton has problems to his left as well, with the death of his ambitious health care plan and a planned welfare reform which would delight traditional conservatives, but anger progressives and minorities. It will be a difficult balancing act to placate alienated moderates while maintaining his popularity within the Democratic Party.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1996 election.

The pollsters will say this was always expected, but victory feels just as sweet. The one unfortunate note is your failure to cross the 50% line, meaning Republicans have retained their control of Congress, and the country will effectively be under minority rule for eight years. The road ahead is unclear, with Medicare, Social Security, and education all remaining top issues, but perhaps you can work out a deal with Gingrich and leave the country in good hands with your successor in four years.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1996 election.

Defeat is a bitter pill to swallow after the Republican Revolution of 1994, Gingrich's antics, and the seemingly endless wave of scandals that bogged down your presidency. At the very least, it seems the country is in trusted hands for the next four or eight years with Bob Dole. Perhaps he'll make progress on immigration, trade deals, and welfare where you couldn't? Unfortunately, it seems this is the end of the road on your turbulent political career. Maybe the Democrats will nominate Hillary next time?
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! Nobody won the 1996 election.

With Ross Perot's declining popularity, nobody saw this coming. As the House prepares to convene to select the next President, all eyes are on the billionaire Texan. No matter what, he's going to be wheeling-and-dealing every member of Congress to gain that extra inch. With the House in the iron grip of Newt Gingrich, your chances of pulling out a victory here are slim, but when has that stopped you before?

fields.description:
For years, Bob Dole has been talked about as a presidential candidate. Finally gaining the nomination this year, the Senate mainstay has a difficult task in front of him. With his party romping to a landslide in the 1994 midterms, Dole, along with the wily Newt Gingrich, now face the impossible job of governing rather than remaining a perpetual opposition party. Much of Dole’s chances this year rest on whether Congress can deliver for the American people.

It will remain a Herculean task to keep the Republican Party intact through the divisive primaries in order to stand a chance of unseating the incumbent President. But with his wartime heroism and decades in office, Dole can make a convincing case that he’s a more reliable figure than Clinton, who remains dogged by ethics and personal scandals, even though Dole’s age remains a top issue for voters.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You won the 1996 election.

It was a bitter fight to the very end, but you did it. After a lifetime of public service, you will become the oldest President to start a first term in American history. Of course, this comes with plenty of implications for 2000 and the future of the Republican Party. Will it follow in Newt Gingrich's radical direction? Or will your own administration prove such a success that everyone will race to take a page out of your book?

Either way, it seems the country was sick after just four years of Bill Clinton. Maybe it was his overreach with his healthcare reform, or his actions during the shutdown, or maybe just enough scandals to finally break through? For now, you'll leave those questions to the prognosticators. You've got plenty to prepare for before January 20th, 1997.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1996 election.

This is a disappointing blow after you started with such a wide lead. During the final weeks, as Clinton's scandals mounted, many thought you could pull it off, but it seems it just wasn't in the cards this year. The recriminations within the party will likely spare you most of the blame, but still, even with Gingrich's antics and the baggage of the religious right, for a moment, you thought you could pull it off.

As Clinton prepares for a second term, he'll no doubt try to find a way to lower the budget deficit and turn the temperature down on the chaos of the past four years. Whether he'll be successful in doing that is an open question, but for the first time in decades, you'll have almost no role to play in it. With your advanced age, another run in 2000 is unthinkable. But maybe Elizabeth could give it a shot?
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! Nobody won the 1996 election.

This is quite the shock after such a bitter campaign. Many of your fellow Republicans will blame Perot for playing spoiler, but it's clear the onus was on you to win a majority. Without that, the House of Representatives will convene to decide the winner.

Given Congress' Republican control, it's a near-certainty that you'll win the presidency via a contingent election. But don't expect any smooth sailing. Liberals will be furious at your victory via a technicality, the sixth Republican win in the past eight presidential elections. It'll take a lot to prove your basic legitimacy in office, let alone settling the difficult issues you'll face with the economy and world affairs.

fields.description:
With his stunning entry on to the American political scene in 1992, Texas billionaire Ross Perot now has his work cut out for him. By blowing past the threshold to approve federal matching funds, Perot’s newly christened Reform Party has an infusion of cash to run a strong presidential campaign in 1996. The only problem is that they don’t have a candidate.

After getting turned down by Bill Bradley and Colin Powell, Perot gave up the game of shopping around for another man, and accepted his role as the face of America’s largest third party in decades. But outside Reform’s diehards, Perot finds his standing from four years ago rapidly dissipating. With his unpopular stances on NAFTA and a growing reputation as a perennial candidate, Perot will not only have to match his previous performance to save face, he’s got to keep the dream of a third party alive.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
What?! You won the 1996 election?

Nobody's sure how you did it. After your precipitous decline from your heights of the Summer of '92, this has to be the greatest political upset in history.

With the markets crashing in the wake of your victory and Washington reeling, it may be best to announce a coalition government to ease concerns. Or just be your usual self and watch what happens? Either way, you have a mountain of problems ahead of you, and no easy answers. It's far harder to govern than it is to be a perpetual change candidate.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Oh no! You didn't even get 5% of the vote.

Even the grimmest prognostications didn't see this one coming. It was taken as a given that you'd cross the threshold to secure the necessary federal matching funds for 2000—albeit half of what Democrats and Republicans receive—but it seems that just wasn't to be.

The reckoning will come swift, with Lamm likely receiving his fair share of the blame for stirring up discontent within the Reform movement, but by this point it's all useless. It seems you're destined to go down in history as a fluke candidate who tapped into something real in 1992 but lost it almost as quickly. Maybe you can go back to the private sector?
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! Nobody won the 1996 election?

This is a stunning result. It seems Clinton had such a divisive first term, the country couldn't even settle on one candidate to elect!

With the House of Representatives convening ahead of a contingent election, all eyes are on Dole and Clinton, not you. Sure, partisans blame you for being a 'spoiler,' but come on, everyone knows you weren't relevant enough for that. Right?

fields.description_as_running_mate:
Al Gore is the ultimate company man. Serving four thankless years as second fiddle to President Bill Clinton, all expect the former Tennessee Senator to be biding his time until 2000, keeping a low profile for now. But this year, Gore is angling for an elevated status as not just Vice President, but an almost co-President. While he eschews all speculation of future campaigns, Gore is clearly hoping that his strength in the South and Baby Boomer youth will come in handy against an aging Dole, and win him some favor within the party.

On a personal note, Gore has served his duties as Vice President with little fuss or bad press, despite his long-rumored bad blood with the First Lady. Hillary will no doubt be a valuable asset for the President as the Clinton campaign heats up, so Gore’s presence may complicate matters.

After New York Congressman Jack Kemp’s announcement last year that he would not seek the presidency, the seas parted for Dole’s candidacy. The two have been on opposite sides of the Republican Party’s ideological divide over budgeting—Dole prioritizes shrinking the deficit over cutting taxes, while Kemp is a staunch free market idealist who emphasizes cutting taxes above all else.

While beloved by the GOP’s conservative faithful—he was Pat Buchanan’s preferred candidate in 1988—Kemp is somewhat at odds with the increasingly rightward drift of the party on social issues. Kemp has criticized the Republican Congress’ welfare plan, supported Affirmative Action, and has sought to expand the party base to the poor and minorities. All of that makes Kemp a highly risky pick, and that’s before even getting to the long-running feud between him and Dole.

Arizona Senator John McCain seems to be a highly attractive candidate for the Vice Presidency. A Vietnam War hero who spent years inside the infamous “Hanoi Hilton,” McCain comes from Navy pedigree, and has taken aggressive stances on foreign policy issues during his time on the Armed Services Committee.

But that’s where the positives end. McCain was a member of the infamous “Keating Five,” raising hackles of corruption, and which would no doubt be resurfaced by Clinton’s ad men, to say nothing of Perot’s populist grandstanding against “special interests.” His awkward closeness to President Clinton on the issue of Vietnam normalization would also need an explanation. So would McCain’s “maverick” streak of independence, which often pits him against his own party, on issues ranging from pork barrel projects to Affirmative Action, and often against Bob Dole.

South Carolina Governor Carroll Campbell has been in the running for Dole’s Vice President since day one, making it known that he’s happy to play ball on just about every issue, with one glaring exception: abortion. Campbell is loath to cross the GOP’s vocal pro-life faction, and his record as Governor has endeared him to that all-important wing of the party.

Outside of Moral Majority circles, Campbell is a bit of an unknown, but the Clinton campaign would be certain to pillory him as just another right-winger closing off the party to minorities, the poor, and moderates. But if Dole seeks to win the south, it’ll take some doubling down on his own conservative credentials. Campbell is also well-versed in the rough-and-tumble of politics, having played an important role on both of George Bush’s presidential campaigns.

Massachusetts Governor Bill Weld has been on the shortlist of his party’s “rising stars” for what feels like a lifetime. Running for state Attorney General when he was just 33, and already had experience as a junior counsel on the Nixon impeachment inquiry, Weld quickly rose through the ranks and earned plaudits from Republican Party stalwarts at every step along the way.

That all has the potential to come to a screeching halt, as Weld stares down the barrel of an increasingly hopeless run for the Senate, having earlier sworn off running for Vice President. Weld is now having second thoughts, marketing himself to Dole’s staff as a play for the political center, with his moderate record as Governor of the nation’s bluest state opening up the liberal Northeast to the GOP. But Weld would be an incredibly audacious pick no matter what, and would certainly rile the already unsatisfied right-wing.

Pat Choate is an economist with a PhD from the University of Oklahoma. As a staunch protectionist and an ally of Perot’s during the fight to oppose NAFTA, Choate gained notice as a frequent guest on talk radio to promote Perot’s candidacy, along with his own books, chiefly on foreign lobbyists and imminent fiscal armageddon.

Choate’s selection would be a clear signal that Perot’s star power from four years ago is fast fading. A political novice, and a relative unknown outside the District of Columbia, the press would certainly delight in Perot’s failure to gain a major political figure’s endorsement, like David Boren or Linda Smith.

The highly controversial Colorado Governor Dick Lamm was once thought to be a shoe-in for the top of the Reform ticket in ‘96. On paper a former Democrat, Lamm’s idiosyncratic political beliefs during his time in office garnered him the nickname of ‘Governor Gloom.’ He took that label one step further in a shocking bid for the Reform Party nomination this year, in which he fashioned a platform calling for the privatization of Social Security and abolishing veteran’s pensions.

Such a set of politically poisonous stances would make Lamm anathema to every voter outside of Perot’s most fervent supporters. But if the Texan wants to get this show on the road and paper over any internal divisions within the Reform Party ahead of the campaign, there’s an argument that Lamm may be the right choice.

Lowell Weicker, the disaffected centrist and longtime Connecticut Republican, would make an intriguing choice for Vice President. His bipartisan cred on Capitol Hill could go a long way towards gaining back whatever’s left of Perot’s respectability from 1992. But Weicker comes with his fair share of risks too.

With an enormous ego, it’s questionable whether Weicker would ever subordinate himself as a number two, and would likely demand enormous concessions from Perot, amounting to essentially a “co-presidency.” Additionally, Weicker’s support for Lamm in the Reform Party’s nominating contest and his own considerations of running would complicate the picture, making Perot’s tightrope walk that much harder. Not to mention that Weicker burned whatever support he had from mainstream Republicans a longtime ago.

On paper, Ohio Representative Marcy Kaptur would make a fantastic choice for Vice President. With over a decade of fending off strong challenges from Republicans in her own district, Kaptur has a solid electoral record. Her staunch opposition to her own President’s NAFTA and GATT agreements would only sweeten the deal.

But the seven-term Congresswoman would not settle for anything less than unconditional surrender. As her terms for agreeing to join what is an all-but doomed third party bid, which would crater her standing within the Democratic Party, Kaptur would demand full rights to craft the Reform Party’s platform, zero commitment to actually campaign for Perot, and a guarantee that her liberal stances on hot-button issues like abortion would become the party line.

fields.description:
Richard Nixon enters the 1972 campaign as the incumbent, after winning the presidency in the chaotic 1968 election. He has governed as a moderate Republican, visiting China and taking a liberal stance on some economic issues.

But Nixon still faces the divisive issues that plagued Johnson four years ago, with his positions on the Vietnam War and crime activating the Democrats' liberal base. Can he make the case that he's the true peace candidate who can finally move the nation beyond the difficult years of the 1960s?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1972 election.

The press will say this was always expected, but don't let them get you down. The campaign was hard-fought, and you gave it your all.

As long as you keep an eye on this Watergate business and keep the economy humming along, your successor should be able to make an argument for four more years in 1976.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1972 election.

This is the result nobody saw coming. Whether it was the press' fixation on Watergate, Democratic dirty tricks from the Kennedys, or just an economy slowing down, this is a painful result to swallow.

McGovern will have his hands full these next four years, and it seems a long time in public office for you has come to an end. Maybe you can write your memoirs in Key Biscayne and settle into a quiet retirement.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Nobody won the 1972 election?

This comes as a shock to everyone. Whether it was the South's dirty tricks or your own strategy of exploiting the country's divisions, it seems nobody knows who the next President will be.

But after Congress has been a thorn in your side these last four years, you fear your time in public service is up. Perhaps you can move back to California with Pat and the girls and enjoy a quiet retirement.

fields.description:
George McGovern has served in the Senate for nine years and ran a brief campaign in 1968 after the death of Bobby Kennedy. A liberal Democrat, McGovern is known for his dovish stance on Vietnam and some controversial economic proposals. He enters the race at a strong disadvantage.

After a divisive primary against Hubert Humphrey and George Wallace, McGovern needs to really shake up the race if he is to have any chance to win. Can he make the case that he's the right man to heal the bitter divisions of the Nixon years?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Wow! You have won the 1972 election!

Even your staunchest supporters can hardly believe this one. Nobody quite knows how you did it. Was it populist backlash over rising inflation? Nixon's own lingering trust problem? Or the seemingly endless war in Vietnam? Only one thing's for certain, and that's that you better get ready to move into the White House this January.

As President, you'll have to disentangle America from Southeast Asia, but perhaps more importantly, revive the floundering economy. If you manage to do both of those without triggering any further crises, you might be in a good position for re-election in 1976. But that's easier said than done.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1972 election.

This was always the likeliest outcome, but it still stings. It seems your incredible organizational skills and passionate base from the Democratic primaries couldn't be replicated against Dick Nixon. The recriminations from inside the party will be swift, and Democrats will almost certainly nominate a more mainstream candidate against Agnew or Connally in 1976.

As for you, your presidential aspirations are likely done, barring any unforseen crisis. In the meantime, you can still return to your Senate with your head held high. That seat is probably yours as long as you want it.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Nobody won the 1972 election?

This comes as a shock to everyone. As the Democratic-controlled Congress scrambles to elect the next President via a contingent election, all eyes are on you. It's unlikely the crucial Southern bloc of the Democratic Party will ever elevate you to the White House, but who knows, maybe you can work out some kind of deal? Stranger things have happened.

But for now, you've got no time to rest. Nixon is sure to throw every last dirty trick in the book at you from now until January. So be prepared, and good luck! You may just emerge from this as President of the United States.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
Spiro Agnew is the current Vice President of the United States and former governor of Maryland. With his hardline rhetoric and theatrical antics arguably costing the Republicans valuable seats in the 1970 midterms, Nixon has a choice to make.

Every vote counts, even in a landslide year. Keeping Agnew on the ticket would please conservatives, but if the election gets close, there may be no room for his big mouth. Is the tradeoff worth it?

John Connally is the Secretary of the Treasury and the former Governor of Texas. His work during the Bretton Woods fiscal crisis made him a household name. As the Democrat closest to the President, there are few spokesmen who would serve Nixon better than Connally.

But the moderate Democrats repelled by McGovern's radical campaign may equal the staunch conservatives infuriated by Nixon rejecting Agnew for a Democrat. Is such a risky gamble worth it when Nixon enjoys a wide lead in every poll?

Rogers Morton is Secretary of the Interior and former chair of the Republican National Committee. Serving as a Congressman from Maryland for eight years, and with his father's political roots in Kentucky, Morton could be an asset for the President in the border states. His strong party connections can also only benefit Nixon.

But as a staunch liberal Republican who endorsed Rockefeller in 1968, Morton would be anathema to the right-wing. Is it worth dropping Agnew for an unknown quantity?

Ronald Reagan is the Governor of California and a conservative darling. With his background in Hollywood, Reagan would surely provide some much-needed charisma for the Nixon campaign. He's also got proven experience after winning re-election in 1970 following a tumultuous first term.

But choosing Reagan may narrow Nixon's support. It seems unnecessary to alienate moderates and liberal Republicans in a year when the polls show the President gaining so many. But who cared about Agnew anyway?

Thomas Eagleton is the four-year incumbent Senator from Missouri. He wasn't initially considered a candidate for running mate, but his status as a moderate Catholic with union ties makes him an appealing suggestion. His known support for the Humphrey campaign is expected to help mend intra-party divides, and he is one of the few Democrats who is willing and eager to appear with McGovern on the ticket.

Young, Catholic, and a party boss favorite, Eagleton appears to be an ideal choice to bring the party together after the McGovern takeover, but little is known about his private life.

Kevin White has been the mayor of Boston since 1968. In a turbulent time for mayors across the country, he was one of the few to defuse the post-King assassination tensions without widespread rioting. He has proven himself as a liberal electoral force in his own right by dispatching ardent anti-busing opposition in both of his campaigns.

White has been a shortlisted running mate for some time, and would deliver inroads with the Catholic and union votes that your campaign is struggling with. One major opponent to his candidacy is Ted Kennedy, who considers him a rival and is fervently against his selection.

Abe Ribicoff is the Senator from Connecticut and a close friend of the Kennedys, but he is best known for his on-stage denunciation of Mayor Richard Daley's police tactics during the disastrous Chicago convention in 1968. As a longtime opponent of the Vietnam War and a well-established liberal ally of yours, he brings experience and gravitas to the ticket and would be the first Jewish Vice President.

Ribicoff is a top choice for the position, but his disinterest in higher office and the recent passing of his wife has made him unwilling to sign on without a guarantee that little campaigning will be expected from him. Additionally, he would be no help with the Catholic vote, and party leaders like Mayor Daley would be displeased.

Patrick Lucey is the serving Governor of Wisconsin and has overseen the transformation of the state from a Republican stronghold into a political battleground. He is considered a liberal Democrat on policy, and is an inoffensive option who will neither excite nor disappoint many in the party.

Lucey is little-known nationally but has proven himself as an effective operator in his home state. He is a Catholic and should help earn their support, but your advisors are concerned that he isn't enough of a home-run swing to change the nature of the campaign.

fields.description:
Dwight Eisenhower is a war hero and the incumbent President. His time in office has been defined by domestic tranquility and reducing the threat of another World War. At home, he has pursued middle-of-the-road answers to the problems of the day, scaling back the New Deal in select industries while making use of government authority in others, to the dismay of some in his party.

Observers believe the election is Eisenhower's to take on a silver platter, although with the President's advanced age and general absence from the public eye, it could prove more complicated than it seems.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1956 Presidential Election.

While it was a foregone conclusion, it was nevertheless fairly earned. You'll return to the White House for another four years, hopefully with a Congress willing to enact your agenda. You are ineligible to run again in 1960, to the delight of the Democrats. Will Richard Nixon finally have his chance to win the White House? Or will one of your preferred candidates pull the rug on him? Either way, the Democrats have been sent to undergo a soul-searching once more, with speculation running high that Senator Kennedy may make a go for it next time around.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1956 Presidential Election.

This is quite the embarrassment for you and your allies. Maybe this was inevitable given your advanced age and declining health, or perhaps the public just didn't trust your judgment this time around. Either way, you'll still be leaving office as a national hero, fondly remembered for your service in World War 2. Where your party goes after your loss is a mystery. They never truly had your back, and with your reputation ruptured from this loss, it seems likely party conservatives will be behind the wheel in 1960 with a man like Bill Knowland.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No candidate captured an Electoral College majority.

This is quite a confusing outcome, truly; no one knows who will benefit most from this decision. Democrats hold slim majorities in both chambers, and it's not out of the question that a deal could be cracked to elevate you and your running mate in return for some political favors. The biggest heartbreak from this result comes from the northern liberals, who came so close to a victory yet so far.

fields.description:
Adlai Stevenson is the former Governor of Illinois and the previous Democratic nominee for the Presidency. Since his loss, he has spent the last four years building his resume, touring the world, and campaigning vigorously for his party in the midterms. The nomination was supposed to be Stevenson's for the taking, though the decline of Eisenhower's health lured opponents into what became a bitterly contested primary.

Stevenson's path to the White House is slim to none, and his defeatism has discouraged him from mounting a serious campaign, although he will gladly speak to a greater cause of liberalism.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1956 Presidential Election.

Wow! You've managed to pull off an upset of a magnitude higher than Truman did just 8 years ago. With, quite literally, the world against you, this achievement is nothing short of a miracle. How you'll govern is up to you. With a firmly Democratic Congress, you should have no trouble enacting said agenda. Globally, you'll surely find an ally in the Soviet Union, perhaps beginning to draw the Cold War to an end. As for 1960, judging by your instincts, you should be a shoo-in, especially if the Republicans nominate your favorite punching bag, Vice President Nixon.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1956 Presidential Election.

This is just about what you expected. You knew the public wasn't on your side, though you can take solace in being every voter's second choice. Given the insurmountable odds, your political career doesn't have to end here. You could continue to travel the world and position yourself as a shoo-in for the next Democratic administration, or maybe you'll try your luck against whoever the Republicans put up in 1960.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No candidate captured an Electoral College majority.

Your allies have to be as frustrated as you are. Having come so close to an outright victory, but split down the middle, whether from a tie or a successful southern splinter. Your first order of business is to prevent any deals that'll see President Eisenhower elected by the Democratic House. From now until January, it seems you'll be getting extra familiar with Speaker Rayburn and Leader Johnson.

fields.description_as_running_mate: Richard Nixon is the current Vice President and, before that, a Senator from California. During the 1952 campaign, he caused quite a stir with allegations of corruption, and since then has been denied a major voice in your administration. He is not your ideal governing partner and will likely be made an issue during the campaign by the Democrats.

fields.description: Put description here
fields.description_as_running_mate: Henry Cabot Lodge is your former campaign manager and your current Ambassador to the United Nations. While he is not your preferred candidate to replace Vice President Nixon, he has his fans, particularly among the liberal Republicans leading the charge to oust him. By selecting him, you will be signalling that you will be running a more liberal campaign compared to 1952.

fields.description: Put description here
fields.description_as_running_mate: While he is an unknown to most of the country, Secretary of the Treasury Robert Anderson is your personal choice for running mate. You would cause a stir by selecting him for the role, as he is quite conservative and a southerner, two things you surely will have to answer for during the campaign.

fields.description: Put description here
fields.description_as_running_mate: Estes Kefauver has run against you for the nomination twice. He is a Senator from Tennessee and an electric campaigner. While he excited liberal voters, there is no love lost for him from the party establishment, who hold resentment towards him over his investigations into urban corruption. Despite that, enthusiasts in your camp believe your pairing with him will be the best chance to win.

fields.description: Rich kid
fields.description_as_running_mate: Senator John F. Kennedy has been a rising star in the party since his victory over Eisenhower pointman Henry Cabot Lodge in 1952. He takes flexible positions on the issues of the day, fitting with your own record, and has even curried favor with the South during the running mate selection process. It remains to be seen whether his religion will be an issue for voters.

fields.description: Put description here
fields.description_as_running_mate: Albert Gore is the top preference of the party establishment. He is a moderate senator from Tennessee and has no grudges with any major party faction, despite his abstaining from the Southern Manifesto. Despite his moderate record, you will be expected to take a conservative stance on civil rights and the economy to reap the benefits of his selection in the south and the west.

fields.description: Put description here
fields.description_as_running_mate: Hubert Humphrey is a Senator from Minnesota and introduced the infamous Civil Rights plank at the 1948 convention. You're in quite a bind if he's not selected as he has been under the assumption you gave him the nod already to be your running mate. Should you be paired with him this fall, you will certainly open yourself up for a challenging campaign in the south and be expected to take a firm pro-civil rights stance.

fields.description:
Since defeating Jimmy Carter in a landslide four years ago, President Reagan has presided over a tumultuous recovery from the stagflation of the 1970s that is just now beginning to bear fruit. His personal charm has thus far allowed him to paper over any controversy that his staunch conservatism may stir up.

Accounting for a formidable electoral firewall in the Sun Belt and the divided opposition, advisors currently recommend that Reagan take a hands-off approach to the campaign. Will their confidence pay off in November?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You won the 1984 election!

This was the expected outcome, but the taste of victory is still sweet. The success of your reelection candidacy has affirmed the efficacy of an optimistic, image-based campaign even in the face of Walter Mondale’s lecturing.

Very few, yourself included, have considered what’s in store for your second term as President. As long as mission creep doesn’t get the better of your capable staff, you’ll be in a good position to hand the White House off to a Republican like George Bush or Howard Baker in four years.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1984 election.

Even with the revelation of the CIA’s murder manual and a series of poor debate performances, almost nobody saw defeat on the horizon. Your time in national politics has almost certainly come to an end.

Walter Mondale will waste no time enacting liberal priorities like a nuclear freeze and deficit reduction, much to your dismay. Of course you hope America will prosper under his presidency, but you’re also eager to believe a conservative like Jack Kemp can take back the White House in 1988–with or without your involvement.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Nobody has won the 1984 election!

The electoral college has tied for the first time in over a hundred years. The race will now go to the House of Representatives, where Democrats have an advantage, but maybe you can convince enough Southerners you're more palatable to their interests than Mondale?

fields.description:
Walter Mondale was Vice President under Jimmy Carter and before that a well-regarded Senator from Minnesota. A New Dealer in the mold of his mentor Hubert Humphrey, Mondale won this year’s primary with strong backing from labor and the Democratic establishment.

Despite his impressive resume, Mondale is seen as adhering to an outmoded brand of liberalism and has faced criticism for his connections to divisive special interests. He will need to find firm footing on any number of critical issues to make a dent in President Reagan’s Teflon persona this Fall.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You won the 1984 election!

Even you didn’t expect this outcome going into election night. Your emphasis on the issues has triumphed over Reagan’s Pollyannish view of the country. Make sure to brush up on policy, because the new Democratic majority in the Senate is eager to get to work enacting the promises you made.

Noting the salience of Reagan’s age in the campaign, Republicans are already hard at work diminishing the importance of your mandate. Still, they are on the backfoot after this shocking result–if all goes well, you’re in good shape to beat Bob Dole in four years.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1984 election.

It’s hard to say you didn’t see it coming, but this loss will take years to get over. Despite his shallow campaign, Reagan will paint his victory as a renewed mandate for conservatism, and the Democratic Party is already rushing to distance itself from New Deal liberalism. It’s likely that Gary Hart will be the nominee in four years, barring an unmitigated catastrophe.

For the first time in your life, you are truly a private citizen. Even as the Democrats disavow you, you command the respect of a generation of liberals–maybe your influence will earn you an ambassadorship or cabinet position in the future.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Nobody has won the 1984 election!

For the first time in over a hundred years, no candidate has won a majority of electoral votes. The race now goes to the House of Representatives. On paper, you're favored in the Democrat-controlled chamber, but Reagan is already making overtures to more conservative members of the caucus. Good luck!

fields.description_as_running_mate: George Bush is the incumbent Vice President. Reagan's former rival has defined his new role as deferential almost to a fault, and will continue loyally in his service as long as he believes it will pay off in four years.

Geraldine Ferraro represents relatively conservative areas of Queens in the House of Representatives. A favorite of Tip O’Neill, Ferraro has developed a reputation as a moderate willing to buck Democratic orthodoxy on divisive issues like busing and crime.

Interest groups and campaign advisors alike recommend that Mondale shake up the race by picking a woman. Despite a limited national profile, Ferraro would please liberals while also appealing to socially conservative Reagan Democrats. However, the Mondale campaign has had little time to fully vet Ferraro’s personal and family finances.

Dianne Feinstein is the incumbent Mayor of San Francisco. A popular Democrat in Reagan's home state, Feinstein raises the possibility of winning California and scrambling the President’s electoral math.

Feinstein has been very openly angling for the vice presidential slot as the Democratic Party convenes in her hometown, and would please women's groups. On the other hand, Mondale would rather not give Reagan an opportunity to tag him as a “San Francisco liberal.”

Gary Hart gave Mondale a run for his money during the surprisingly narrow Democratic primaries. A Senator from Colorado and one-time campaign manager for George McGovern, Hart represents a new breed of Atari Democrats more concerned with technological advancement than traditional liberal wedge issues.

After the lengthy nomination contest, Hart’s selection would go a long way to bridge the gap between Mondale’s campaign and younger, Reagan-friendly suburbanites. However, he would demand several policy concessions if he were to join the ticket, and offers little to supporters of Jesse Jackson.

Jesse Jackson was also a thorn in Mondale’s side during the acrimonious Democratic primary. The self-proclaimed heir to the late Dr. King, Jackson commanded wide swaths of the African American vote despite running a distant third.

Jackson has kept Mondale on edge in the buildup to the Convention by threatening to withhold his endorsement unless he is considered for the Vice Presidency, but the Reverend’s past comments about New York’s Jewish community leave many in the inner circle wondering whether his selection would be more trouble than it’s worth. Older Black leaders are also skeptical Jackson motivates African American voters as effectively as he claims.

fields.description:
George Bush won a thin popular mandate in 2000, and the last four years have been eventful to say the least. An attack on the WTC in 2001 led to Bush declaring a War on Terror, which has expanded into a controversial War in Iraq. On the domestic front, Bush has passed the largest tax cuts in history, and overhauls of education and healthcare.

Bush has strong support within his own party, and can use moral issues to motivate his base in key swing states. He also has broad approval on his War on Terror. However, his domestic policy is more controversial compared to Kerry’s, and most Americans trust Kerry to better lead the economy than Bush.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2004 election.

Despite a close challenge from John Kerry, you have secured a second term for your presidency.

You’ll stabilize Iraq in your second term, and hopefully pass that gay marriage amendment. As for the economy, you can renew your efforts to privatize Social Security. The economy will hopefully improve and could be booming by the end of your term, so long as that housing bubble doesn’t pop in catastrophic fashion. If all the above happens, you will leave a strong legacy to your successor.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2004 election.

Considering the policies and events of your first term, it seems like they were just too controversial to get re-elected.

Expect John Kerry to rescind your tax cuts and seek a new foreign policy with our allies. Hopefully your brother Jeb or some other Republican will present a strong challenge to him in 2008. As for you, you are still popular within your party, so your political career isn’t necessarily over.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! You have won in a squeaker.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, marking the first time this has happened since 1824. Fortunately for you, the majority of U.S. states have Republican controlled congressional delegations, and they will cast their votes accordingly.

Given the incredibly close nature of the election, you will surely be expected to govern in a more moderate fashion than you have done so far.

fields.description:
John Kerry is a Vietnam war veteran, and a Senator from Massachusetts. He won many awards during his time as a serviceman, including three purple hearts.

John Kerry has a popular domestic agenda when it comes to healthcare and the economy, and can use his history as a serviceman to burnish his credentials on national security. However, he will have to finesse the issue of the War on Terror, which Bush remains popular on, and attacking Bush too hard on it or the war in Iraq may fuel allegations of him being a “flip-flopper.”
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2004 election.

You were able to defeat George Bush and win back the Presidency.

You will repeal Bush’s tax cuts in order to reduce the deficit, and to pay for a new expansive healthcare policy. Perhaps you can also push for more progressive policies on gay marriage and abortion. As for foreign policy, hopefully you can withdraw from Iraq and restore foreign faith in the United States. Given no unexpected disasters, you will probably be able to win reelection in 2008.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2004 election.

Despite your efforts, it seems like you just weren’t up to the task of defeating Bush.

Bush will continue the war in Iraq no matter how controversial it becomes, and will continue to alienate American allies with his War on Terror. There are murmurs within the party of you running again in 2008, but who knows what will happen in the next few years.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost in a squeaker.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, for the first time since 1824. Unfortunately for you, a majority of states have Republican controlled congressional delegations.

Considering how close this election was, Bush will definitely be expected to govern in a more bipartisan manner.

fields.description:
Ralph Nader enters the 2000 election as the Green candidate after years as an activist and consumer advocate.

After eight years of Bill Clinton, it is clear that the United States needs a true liberal alternative -- one that will fight for fair trade, universal health care, free college, and campaign finance reform. Nader's primary goal in this election is to win 5% of the popular vote, which will qualify the Green Party for federal matching funds in 2004.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2000 election.

This was definitely not supposed to happen. Good luck!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
As expected, you have lost the 2000 election.

The legacy of this campaign depends on a couple of factors. First of all, did you receive 5% of the popular vote? If so, congratulations! You will enable the Green Party to run a vigorous campaign in 2004 and present a true choice to the American people. Also, the Democrats were a little peeved that you "stole" votes from them in this election. Hopefully that doesn't lead to a backlash.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! No candidate received 270 electoral votes, but the House will elect George W. Bush as President.

Did you receive 5% of the popular vote? If so, congratulations! You will enable the Green Party to run a vigorous campaign in 2004 and present a true choice to the American people. Also, the Democrats were a little peeved that you "stole" votes from them in this election. Hopefully that doesn't lead to a backlash, especially since they will lose the vote in the House.

fields.description_as_running_mate: Dick Cheney is the current Vice President, former CEO of Halliburton, and former Secretary of Defense under your father. Picking him will be the safe, expected choice.

Bill Frist is the Senate Majority Leader and is from the state of Tennessee. He is fairly moderate and has some gravitas on healthcare. He would be a safe pick to be your running mate. However, picking him could be detrimental since Dick Cheney is also a safe pick, and you would lose support for changing VPs.

The world renowned former Mayor of New York City, Rudy Giuliani is popular among nearly every voter nationwide. He would also burnish national security related issues and is very eager to campaign. He will be of great assistance in gaining swing voters. However, he is known to have a troubled marital past, he will hurt among conservative voters, and you would appear indecisive on changing away from Cheney.

Colin Powell is the Secretary of State and maybe the only one who can compete with Giuliani in terms of nationwide popularity. He will help your national security credentials and has little personal baggage. Powell will also help with Hispanic and Black voters. However, Powell could hurt you among the conservative base, and you will appear indecisive by dumping Cheney.

John Edwards is the outgoing Senator from North Carolina. Even though Howard Dean got the most attention, it was Edwards who was second to you in the primaries. Edward is the more or less the expected pick, and could add youth and energy to the ticket. However, he won’t really have any big electoral impact.

Bob Graham has gained renown for his national security expertise after the 9/11 attacks and voted against the Iraq War, which will help solidify your liberal base. He is also from the key state of Florida, which if you win, will almost certainly hand you the election. However, if you don’t win it, he will be of little addition to the ticket.

Dick Gephardt is the former House Majority Leader and was a key ally of President Clinton. A moderate, who is heavily pro-labor, Gephardt can be a big help in his home of Missouri and tip the scales in the Industrial Midwest in states like Iowa and Ohio. However, he has been a outspoken advocate of gay rights which could be a small issue in the Industrial Midwest, though his pro-labor stance will likely overcome it. You and Gephardt also have different views on NAFTA which could potentially make you appear a bit indecisive.

Wesley Clark was a contender for the Democratic nomination, and a close ally of the Clintons. He will fend off all accusations about the Democrats’ “weak on defense” stereotype and will help ease potential attacks against you testifying against Vietnam or other things regarding Vietnam. However, in the Clinton Administration he was known as a quasi-hawk, and there are doubts about his views on Iraq and other policies. He will also not really bring any big electoral advantage anywhere.

Winona LaDuke is a Native American activist of Ojibwe ancestry. She lives in Minnesota and has been active in attempts to regain land that once belonged to various American Indian tribes. She has written a book and started organizations in support of this issue.

fields.description:
Barack Obama is the Junior Senator from Illinois. His swift political rise began with his keynote speech at the 2004 Democratic National Convention, and concluded with a stunning victory in the primaries, upsetting the frontrunner Hillary Rodham Clinton. Obama presents himself as the face of a new generation, drawing comparisons with John F. Kennedy. Politically positioned as a mainstream liberal, he would be the nation’s first black President.

To win, Obama must harness his image as a standard bearer of hope and change, having already dazzled crowds at home and around the world. He will have to define his positions on the Iraq War, the Great Recession, and other issues of the time -- playing up his readiness for office without dampening support from moderates with the liberal positions his base expects him to adopt.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Yes We Can!

Some people thought it inevitable, but that does nothing to take away from the historic nature of your victory. You are now the first African-American ever elected President in the history of the United States. John McCain calls to congratulate you, and congressional Democrats ride your coattails to strengthen their majority in both chambers.

On the domestic front, the outlook is stormy. You have the political capital to pass sweeping reforms of the finance sector and healthcare. You can go big on your campaign promises, or water them down to appeal to the powerful moderate wing of the Democratic caucus. Good luck with the war in Iraq, and with catching Bin Laden.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2008 election.

This loss is a painful one to take. After all the hype you generated with your astounding primary win, to come up short represents a major failing on your part. President Bush’s numbers are in the tank, the economy is in a rut and the crowds at your rallies were bigger than ever seen before -- and now the world wakes up to the reality of President John McCain.

The second-guessing will be fast and furious. Hillary Clinton is livid with you, having “stolen” her nomination in a perfectly winnable election year. She will probably be the nominee in 2012, if not another rising star like you were once considered. President McCain has a lot of work to do, and his agenda’s success will depend on his relationship with an all-Democratic congress, in which you still hold your Senate seat. Will you make enough waves to run again in four years?
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Yes We Can! Kind of.

This is an entirely bizarre and unexpected situation. On the one hand, you underperformed expectations and have managed to bring about the most unlikely of scenarios, leaving party insiders worried about the strength of your mandate. On the other, the Democrats still have solid control over the House and Senate, and will undoubtedly elevate you to the Presidency, making you America’s first black President.

There’s a chance you’ll have the sting of not winning the popular vote, but if you’re successful maybe you can rectify that in four years as your predecessor did. Congratulations Mr. President, you did it...just barely.

fields.description:
John S. McCain III is a bona fide war hero, and a Senator from Arizona since 1986. Captured during his service in Vietnam, he endured years of torture at the hands of the NVA. Upon his release, he received a hero’s welcome before entering the political arena as a Republican. He made a bid for the Presidency in 2000, losing an acrimonious primary to George Bush.

McCain is known as the “Maverick”, due to his frequent willingness to break with the party on many issues - this can be as much an asset as a liability. He is known for his unorthodox positions on key social issues. To win, McCain can either emphasize his independent streak, or cozy up to the party’s conservative wing. There is also the matter of how closely he should associate himself with George W. Bush to consider - Bush is incredibly unpopular, but straying too far from the administration may hurt you with the base.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2008 election.

In a comeback for the ages, you have beat out Obama’s seemingly unbeatable machine, and reasserted the Republican Party’s dominance in modern America. From the Hanoi Hilton to the White House over the course of forty years, you have made your fellow vets, Arizonans everywhere, and especially your mother, very proud. Obama congratulates you, and your old rival George Bush begins the preparations for you to move into the White House.

You will begin your term with a lot on your plate. The economy is in the ditch, and Democrats still control both houses of Congress. It is now up to you to work with legislators to deliver on the promises you made to the American people. You also have to worry about the situation in Iraq, and catching Bin Laden. But if there’s anyone out there up to the task, it’s the Maverick.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2008 election.

You came to the table with grit, determination, and an indomitable spirit, and you leave the arena with your pride intact. This was the result everyone expected, but that doesn’t mean you should lose hope after coming this far. Obama will go on to make history as America’s first African-American President, governing with a Democratic supermajority in both chambers - the ball’s in his court now.

You’re likely too old to run for President again, but you still have your seat in the Senate, and Arizona loves you. In the days ahead, you will have to work with President Obama to see the country through many crises, from Iraq to the economy. Let’s hope the bipartisan spirit you fostered during the campaign will transfer to the next session of Congress.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2008 election.

In spite of the big-name endorsements and polling advantage, you have defied expectations enough to take the election to the House of Representatives. Unfortunately, President Bush’s unpopularity was a big factor in down-ballot elections, and proved too much to surmount as Democrats have held their majority in both chambers. Accordingly, Barack Obama will become the 44th President of the United States.

You can take solace in the fact that you gave the Democrats a run for their money in what should have been a cakewalk year for them. You will still have an important role to play in the Senate, where Americans expect action after a year of talking. Whatever comes next for the Maverick, you have done your country proud.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
Joseph R. Biden Jr. has represented Delaware for six terms in the Senate, fostering a reputation as a bipartisan dealmaker and presiding over the Anita Hill hearings as Chairman of the Judiciary Committee.

Biden has made two failed presidential campaigns already; now sitting atop the powerful Foreign Relations Committee, Joe Biden would add three decades of experience to your ticket and bridge the gaps in your resumé, especially on foreign policy. Biden is known to occasionally make gaffes which draw media attention; his presence on the stump will be unpredictable.

Tim Kaine is the popular Governor of Virginia, known for his past as a Catholic missionary and Mayor of Richmond. He is seen as an adept micromanager and policy wonk of sorts, and would add an experienced, uncontroversial voice to the ticket.

Kaine is ideologically moderate, and has recently earned positive media coverage for his response to the Virginia Tech shooting, as well as his response on behalf of the party to the 2006 State of the Union address. Picking him might boost you in Virginia, and help bridge a growing gap between the Democratic Party and religious voters.

Evan Bayh is the Junior Senator from Indiana, son of the famous Birch Bayh. He was Indiana’s governor for eight years in the 90s, fostering a reputation as a moderate Democrat with some conservative tendencies, such as supporting capital punishment.

Widely popular within the party, Bayh has stood out as a foreign policy hawk -- going so far as to co-sponsor the Iraq War resolution, which could cause problems with the party base. However, he is well-regarded in Indiana, a state which your advisors believe is possible to win this year.

Kathleen Sebelius is the recently re-elected Governor of Kansas, a popular Democratic leader in an otherwise deeply Republican state. Picking her would give more weight to your message of bipartisanship, and galvanize women voters who were enthusiastic about Hillary Clinton.

Known to be fiscally responsible, with a particular interest in healthcare and education, Sebelius has worked with state Republicans to pass her agenda while maintaining a boldly progressive attitude towards issues like abortion, capital punishment, and the environment. Your advisors believe she would be helpful in the Great Plains - but for all her assets, many are skeptical that Kansas could be in contention by any means.

Chris Dodd is a long-time Senator from Connecticut, currently serving as Chair of the Banking Committee. He boasts solid credentials on the economy, and is an experienced legislator and campaigner. His past could also be a drawback to voters who see him as a big-time insider and are suspicious of his ties to the banking sector.

However, by adopting some of Dodd’s left-leaning positions, picking him could help you make a play for the activist wing of the party. Dodd has emerged as one of the most vocal opponents of the Iraq War and has a record of advocating for labor rights and the decriminalization of marijuana.

Sarah Palin is the popular first-term Governor of Alaska, recommended by many of your closest advisors as a game changing figure who could generate enthusiasm from conservatives and women voters. In her home state she has shaken up the political landscape, taking on party elders and charting her own course. Her patented brand of ‘straight talk’ and speaking her mind has generated many favorable comparisons to you.

Some people in the establishment say Palin is a risky choice, known to be a loose cannon, but the enthusiasm she generates from the party base is undeniable. She would make history as the nation’s first woman Vice President, and lock up Alaska, which looks shaky this year. Her youth, especially in comparison to you, could also be an asset in the face of Obama’s message of change.

Mitt Romney was one of your primary opponents this year, and gave you a run for your money. He is the son of the famous George Romney, and the former Governor of Massachusetts. In addition to his history as CEO of Bain Capital, he was responsible for the success of the 2002 Salt Lake Winter Olympics. His style of conservatism is relatively moderate, having built a successful near-universal healthcare system in Massachusetts, but he has moved more to the right in recent years.

There is no strong opposition to Romney from any corner of the GOP, but some party stalwarts are skeptical of his liberal history on abortion and social issues, despite his apparent shift in views. He would also be the first Mormon Vice President.

Tom Ridge was Pennsylvania’s Governor, credited with many improvements in infrastructure and education. He will certainly improve your chances in that state, and his warm personality might appeal to voters after eight years of Dick Cheney. Ridge is popular within the party as a fellow Vietnam veteran with a tough-on-crime reputation as Governor. He became the first head of the Department of Homeland Security, resigning shortly before the 2004 election.

While Ridge is not a moderate per se, his support of abortion could make things very awkward with the socially conservative base - one silver lining being that this stance might help with Republican women and independents. He is also closely associated with President Bush, a factor that could help or harm your campaign.

Tim Pawlenty is the Governor of Minnesota, where he won plaudits from Republicans for resolving the state’s budget deficit without raising taxes (unless you count cigarettes). He gained the attention of the media last year after a deadly bridge collapse in Minneapolis; while his initial response was widely praised, the political battle which ensued has frustrated his agenda.

Pawlenty is sure to appeal to voters in the upper Midwest, as an able administrator with a young, friendly face that may just put Minnesota in play. Despite his strong conservative credentials, he is seen by many as a moderate, owing to his inchoate image and low profile among voters. He has also come under scrutiny for campaign finance violations, which may be seized upon by Obama.

Joe Lieberman would be the ultimate wild card pick. A Democratic Senator from Connecticut, he is not only an open liberal, but he even ran against Bush in 2000 as Al Gore’s running mate. Despite this, the two of you have become fast friends during your time in congress, and he is the most prominent Democrat to endorse your campaign.

Lieberman is one of the Senate’s most hawkish members - a position which lost him the 2006 primary and forced him to win re-election as an Independent. By choosing him, you would be making a huge gamble: Lieberman is vocally for abortion rights, gay rights, and has a strongly liberal voting record in the Senate. It would be a system shock for the rank and file, and guarantee a hemorrhage in support from the conservative base. But he also presents the chance to reshape the political map to your benefit.

fields.description:
Rutherford B. Hayes is the incumbent Governor of Ohio, serving on and off since 1868. Hayes also served in the Union Army during the Civil War, even being brevetted Major General for his service during the Army of the Shenandoah in the Valley Campaigns of 1864.

Although he has experience and a respectable resume, he is not well known outside of Ohio and thus, he must craft a reputation for himself nationwide. He has been noted as a reformer with support for Civil Rights. Hayes will also have to balance distancing himself from President Grant and the corruption of his administration without completely bolting from some of his more well received ideas.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1876 election.

Despite a strong challenge from Governor Tilden, you will keep the White House under Republican control. Of course, the road ahead is a tough one, as you are faced with cleaning up the corruption and pulling the nation out of this economic slump.

Depending on how your administration faces these issues, you could leave your successor with a strong economy and a clean government. It seems both the Stalwarts and the Half-Breeds are anxious for the 1880 election.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1876 election.

It's hard to say this was unexpected, given Tilden's initial lead. Democrats will still control the House of Representatives, albeit with a reduced margin, while the Senate remains in Republican hands.

Samuel Tilden will be the first Democrat to be elected President since James Buchanan in 1856. It seems that your political career is over -- at least the people of Ohio will remember you fondly.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost in a nail-biter.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, marking the first time this has happened since 1824. Unfortunately for you, the majority of U.S. states have Democratic control the Congressional delegations, and they will cast their votes for Tilden accordingly.

It is unlikely you will have another chance in 1880 -- thus, it seems your political career is over.

fields.description:
Samuel Tilden is the incumbent Governor of New York, leading a Democratic sweep of the statewide offices in the 1874 elections. Tilden supported the Union during the Civil War, which will help him blunt attacks from those waving the bloody shirt around.

Tilden has fought against corruption from the Tammany Hall political machine during his tenure as Governor, and had to overcome incredibly strong opposition from ''Honest John'' Kelly, the leader of Tammany Hall in order to secure the nomination. He starts out as the early favorite to win, due to the unpopularity of the Grant Administration and the lack of reputation of Governor Hayes. Tilden must emphasize his record, attack the corruption in the Grant administration, and balance the interests of the North and South.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1876 election.

While it may have looked close for a bit, neither side seems to doubt your victory. You will be the first Democrat elected to the White House since James Buchanan in 1856. Democrats will retain their control over the House of Representatives, whereas the Senate seems to be held by Republicans very narrowly.

You could likely pass some of your reform-minded policies with support from reformist Republicans. You also are expected to end Reconstruction as soon as possible. If you can pass civil service and other reforms, winning re-election in 1880 will be no trouble at all.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1876 election.

The excited convention that nominated you didn't seem to translate to an electoral win. Hayes now has the chance to give the Republican Party a fresh start with the American people, and hopefully implement similar reforms that you have promised.

If you choose to, renomination in 4 years also isn't out of the question. However, it is more likely that you will likely choose to retire.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! You have won a true nail-biter.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, marking the first time this has happened since 1824. Fortunately for you, the majority of U.S. states have Democratic controlled congressional delegations, and they will cast their votes for you accordingly.

If you can pass civil service and other reforms, winning re-election in 1880 will be no trouble at all. Best of luck, President-elect Tilden.

fields.description: Peter Cooper is the Greenback Party's nominee. It will take an insane amount of spacebarring to get him to victory.
n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate: William Wheeler is a member of the House of Representative from the state of New York. Being from a populus swing state, he may help bring geographic balance to the ticket giving Hayes an edge in a state that is leaning towards its very own Governor Tilden. Winning New York would practically seal an Electoral College win for Hayes, and would likely surprise Tilden, who has expected to win the Empire State.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate: Frederick T. Frelinghuysen is an incumbent Senator from New Jersey, and a member of the well-known Frelinghuysen family. He is considered a Radical Republican, who has taken strong stances on punishing former Confederates. At the same time, he has allied himself with the Stalwart faction, which may hurt Hayes' image of a reformer.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate: Thomas Hendricks is the outgoing governor of Indiana. His presence on the ticket alone will certainly help in the crucial swing state of Indiana. While much of his agenda has been blocked by the Republican-controlled legislature, Hendricks has been noted as a reformer. He also has served as a Senator and Representative, giving him plenty of experience. However, Hendricks is is far more sympathetic to the Greenback cause, which will help or hurt the ticket depending on the state.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate: Winfield Scott Hancock is the Major General and Civil War hero from Pennsylvania, who also sought the Democratic nomination this year. Although he has never held public office, his Union general status can help deflect attacks from those waving the bloody shirt. His most notable service during the Civil War was as a commander at the Battle of Gettysburg. He also has not taken a stance on the money issue. Party leaders would prefer someone such as Hendricks, but if Tilden is looking to win Pennsylvania, having the convention select Hancock will certainly help.

fields.description:
Barack Obama enters the 2012 campaign as the incumbent, having defeated John McCain in the 2008 election. He has governed as a moderate liberal, passing a health care reform program and taking a hawkish stance on some foreign policy issues.

Obama's administration has been dogged by a severe recession and an unconvincing recovery, which he has consistently blamed on the policies of his Republican predecessor and on the obstructionism of his political opponents in Congress.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2012 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Mitt Romney, you have held on to the Presidency.

On the political front, it appears that your health care legislation that was passed in early 2010 will survive and go into effect. While the economy has not yet recovered as strongly as you hoped and promised, you will now have four more years to leave a strong legacy to your Democratic successor.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2012 election.

In spite of your spirited defense, Mitt Romney has won the Presidency. Nearly two centuries after the ill-fated campaign of Joseph Smith, Romney will become America's first Mormon president.

On the political front, it appears that Romney will make a push for more tax cuts to revive the economy. He will also try to repeal your health care law. If your defeat was narrow enough, you may be able to attempt a comeback in 2016.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost in a squeaker.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, marking the first time this has happened since 1824. Unfortunately for you, the majority of U.S. states have Republican controlled congressional delegations, and they will cast their votes for Mitt Romney.

Given the incredibly close nature of the election, you can probably set your sights on a political comeback in 2016, if that is what you desire.

fields.description:
