Your first order of business will be to confirm the annexation of Texas. More generally you can fight for the expansion of the United States in line with the ideals of "Manifest Destiny". With a Democratic majority in Congress, you will have wide latitude to implement your program, after four years of Tyler's paralysis. Best wishes for your term in office.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1844 Election

President Clay is sure to obstruct the annexation of Texas. Hopefully a new President can bring this to a better conclusion in four years. In the meantime, your voice may hold some influence, in an advisory capacity, with the Democratic majority in Congress. It is unlikely, however, that you will be nominated for President over the likes of Lewis Cass, James Buchanan, or others in 1848.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow. No candidate has achieved a majority in the Electoral College

This is surely an unusual situation, given that no candidate besides yourself and Clay seemed poised to win an electoral vote. Fortunately, the Democrats have won a majority in the House and seem likely to confirm you as the ultimate winner. Best wishes for your term in office.

fields.description:
Henry Clay runs in a Presidential election for the third time, and begins as the favorite against Polk. He must quickly define a position on Texas. It will be difficult to do so without alienating some bloc of the Whigs.

Clay would prefer to keep slavery and expansion on the back-burner, and advance his own issues like tariffs, internal improvements, and a national currency. Can he find redemption from his political defeats to Andrew Jackson, and finally break into the White House?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1844 Election

Your first order of business will be to block the annexation of Texas, and hopefully to end the further discussion of this issue. Then you can concentrate on undoing the damage that Andrew Jackson and his followers have inflicted on the American System. Unfortunately, it appears that you will have to deal with a Democratic majority in Congress. Best wishes for these next four years.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1844 Election

President Polk is sure to go through with the annexation of Texas. You can only hope it doesn't lead to war. Even if the U.S. is successful in the short-term, the acquisition of such territory is sure to reopen the slavery question in a way which may hurt the Whigs. As for your own fortunes, you have likely missed your last chance to become President. How will your legacy be remembered?
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow. No candidate has achieved a majority in the Electoral College

This is sure an unusual situation, given that no candidate besides yourself and Polk seemed poised to win an electoral vote. Unfortunately, the Democrats have won a majority in the House and seem likely to confirm James K. Polk as the ultimate winner. How will your legacy be remembered?

fields.description_as_running_mate: George Dallas has served as a Pennsylvania Senator, and as Mayor of Philadelphia. Pennsylvania is a crucial state to win if the Democrats are to return to the White House. Dallas would balance the ticket in two ways. First, he is a Northerner. Secondly, he is a moderate on the issues of tariffs and banking, compared to Polk, Jackson, and most other Southerners. He is not a moderate on the issue of expansion, and would help define that as the central Democratic issue in this election.

Dallas is the preferred choice of the Convention, but Polk could intervene on behalf of Levi Woodbury. Woodbury's reputation is more national than Dallas's, but he also comes from a smaller state. Woodbury has served as Secretary of the Treasury and is much more orthodox on economic issues, favoring a limited view of the federal government's powers. This could galvanize Democrats in the closer states in the South and West, but could also be a hindrance in Pennsylvania and New York.

Theodore Frelinghuysen has served as a Senator from New Jersey, and as Mayor of Newark. He is known as something of an evangelist, being involved in numerous bible societies and advocating for moral uplift. Associates of Frelinghuysen have voiced anti-Catholic sympathies, however. His selection would help with nativists, but exacerbate the Whigs' problems with the Catholic vote. Southerners with a long memory also recall his loud opposition to the Indian Removal Act.

John Sergeant ran with Henry Clay in 1832, and has served in Congress on three occasions. He worked for the Second Bank of the United States, and strongly favors a revival of the national banking system. He is also known as an opponent of slavery, even voting against the Missouri Compromise in 1820. Obviously, this background could help Clay in certain regions, and hurt him in others. Sergeant has also been out of political office for over three years.

Millard Fillmore was an influential Congressman before leaving that body in 1843. He has strongly supported Whig economic policies such as a tariff and national bank. He has taken stances against the expansion of slavery, without veering into the dangerous territory of abolitionism. He is well-connected to New York politics, and his selection would undoubtedly motivate the party in that crucial state.

fields.description: Woodrow Wilson won in a 1912 landslide, and has passed an array of legislation in his first term. In 1916, however, foreign affairs are beginning to dominate. A loud minority of Democrats are aggressively anti-war and expect the same from Wilson. Can Wilson make the case that his passage of an antitrust act, a child labor law, an income tax Amendment, and the Federal Reserve Act, all warrant reelection? His recent remarriage has also fed some gossip.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1916 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Charles Evans Hughes, you have held on to the Presidency.

On the domestic front, it appears that your support of labor and progressivism has been rewarded. Internationally, let's all hope that fears of war with Germany prove to be unfounded.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1916 election.

Maybe 1912 was just an anomaly, brought about by Roosevelt's grandstanding. It has been over 20 years since the Democrats defeated a united Republican Party, and that advantage shows no sign of abating.

On the domestic front, let's hope that your achievements survive. Internationally, no one can say what might happen next. In a novel move, you have offered to do your part by resigning immediately, rather than waiting until March 4th.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No candidate has captured an Electoral College majority.

Elections for Congress have also resulted in an even split among members, and it is extremely unclear who might ultimately win this election. Best of luck in what is sure to be a contentious process.

fields.description: Charles Evans Hughes is the former Governor of New York. He served on the Supreme Court from 1910, until resigning to accept the Republican Nomination. Hughes is a compromise candidate -- he was serving on the Court during the messy 1912 schism. It will be difficult for Hughes to condemn Wilson's legislation without losing support from progressives such as Roosevelt. Many Republicans also favor an aggressive stance against Germany, while others believe Hughes should finesse the issue.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1916 election.

After the tumultuous 1912, the natural supremacy of the Republican Party has reasserted itself. The next steps are up to you -- perhaps you can lead the repeal of the Adamson Act, or replace it with something more measured and comprehensive. In regards to Europe, best of luck in whatever may occur over the next four years. Finally, Wilson plans to resign before your March 4th inauguration, so that you might assume the office now.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1916 election.

Ultimately, the popularity of Woodrow Wilson was just a little much to overcome.

It appears that Wilson's agenda will remain in effect domestically. In world affairs, it remains to be seen how the situation in Europe will finally resolve itself. As to your own prospects, it is unclear what your next steps will be. The Supreme Court seat you once enjoyed has now been lost for the foreseeable future.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No candidate has captured an Electoral College majority.

Elections for Congress have also resulted in an even split among members, and it is extremely unclear who might ultimately win this election. Best of luck in what is sure to be a contentious process.

fields.description_as_running_mate: Thomas R. Marshall has served as Wilson's Vice President since 1913, but the two have had icy relations. However, keeping Marshall on the ticket would preserve party unity and avoid a distracting storyline during the campaign. Marshall was previously the Governor of Indiana and is popular in that state. Politically, he is more moderate than Wilson has been.

Newton Baker has served as Secretary of War since the early part of 1916. Some advisors are encouraging Wilson to replace Marshall with Baker. The two have a much better working relationship, and Baker was formerly the mayor of Cleveland, Ohio. His nomination may help in Ohio, but it would also create headlines and arouse some Marshall supporters.

Charles W. Fairbanks has served as a Senator from Indiana, and as Vice President under Teddy Roosevelt. He was seeking the top of the ticket this year, but has agreed to serve as Vice President a second time. Fairbanks supported William Howard Taft during the split in 1912, and would balance the ticket in a more conservative direction.

Besides Fairbanks, Elmer Burkett is the only candidate for Vice President with significant support, and Hughes could attempt to elevate him. Burkett has served as Representative and Senator from Nebraska, striking a moderate course on many of the labor and economic issues of the day. His region is more in favor of peace, vis a vis Europe, as well. Nationally, he is less well-known than Fairbanks.

fields.description: George Bush has served as Vice President for eight years, and also as a UN Ambassador, Director of the RNC, and Director of the CIA. He is hoping to succeed the popular Reagan, but fights the impression that he is too dependent on his former boss. He must prove he has the independence, ideological rigor, and strength to serve as President, all while finding some way to reduce the popularity of his opponent. Bush appears to be trailing badly as the campaign begins.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1988 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Michael Dukakis, you have held on to succeed Ronald Reagan.

Whatever you did, it must have worked. Observers were leaving your campaign for dead just a few months ago. On the political front, you can continue the policies of Reagan or turn in a more moderate direction. Internationally, you can hopefully oversee a period of relaxed tension with the Soviet Union.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1988 election.

Perhaps it was always a long-shot -- the American people just seemed ready to move on from Reagan.

Time will tell if Dukakis governs as a moderate, a liberal, or a technocrat. A lot can happen in four years, but the early gossip is that Bob Dole has the inside track for the 1992 nomination. Your next steps are unclear.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1988 election.

Although the Electoral College was tied, the Democrats have won a solid majority in the House, and will elevate Michael Dukakis to the Presidency.

Time will tell if Dukakis governs as a moderate, a liberal, or a technocrat. A lot can happen in four years, but the early gossip is that Bob Dole has the inside track for the 1992 nomination. Your next steps are unclear.

fields.description: Michael Dukakis has been elected three times as Governor of Massachusetts. His chances this year seem to be good, if he can press the case for his own ability and challenge the readiness of Bush. Dukakis has won the nomination without aligning himself firmly with a specific wing of the party. His national reputation is positive, but inchoate. He will be expected to define himself more clearly, and may need to explain some older votes and decisions as they become known.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1988 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from George Bush, you have held on to succeed Ronald Reagan.

You were always the favorite to win, but a lot could have gone wrong. On the political front, you can work a Democratic House to overturn the worst excesses of Reagan. Internationally, you can hopefully oversee a period of relaxed tension with the Soviet Union.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1988 election.

In spite of you being the favorite, things just never seemed to click once the real campaigning began.

Time will tell if Bush governs as a moderate, or a staunch conservative. Many Democrats feel that this election was yours to lose, and it seems unlikely that you will be welcome to run again in four years. Your term as Governor, however, runs through 1991.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1988 election.

Although the Electoral College was tied, the Democrats have won a solid majority in the House, and will elevate Michael Dukakis to the Presidency.

On the political front, you can work a Democratic House to overturn the worst excesses of Reagan. Internationally, you can hopefully oversee a period of relaxed tension with the Soviet Union.

fields.description_as_running_mate: Dan Quayle has served as a Senator from Indiana for the past seven years. He would be an unexpected choice, and the first baby boomer to run on a national ticket. He does not have a long record of achievement at the highest stage, but he could have some appeal to social conservatives, Midwesterners, and younger voters. There is some skepticism about his intellect, and his campaigning and debating ability.

Bob Dole was Bush's primary rival for the Republican nomination. He has served as a Senator from Kansas since 1969. He is the preferred choice of many in the party, and has a loyal following on Capitol Hill. Many believe he would help immensely in the farm states. On the other hand, Dole served as Gerald Ford's running mate in 1976, and made some over-the-top attacks on Jimmy Carter which served as a distraction. He and Bush also have lukewarm feelings for each other.

Jack Kemp is a Congressman from New York who has served since the early 1970s. Before that, he was a well-known professional football quarterback. He was one of the main architects and proponents of Reagan's supply-side tax cuts, and is known to be a staunch fiscal conservative. This could cut both ways in a general election. He would be a good choice for most Republicans, and is consistently mentioned as a possible running-mate.

Lloyd Bentsen has served as a Senator from Texas since 1971. In his first Senatorial election, he defeated George Bush. He is viewed as a moderate Democrat, particularly on economic issues. Texas could be a competitive state in the fall, and Bentsen's presence would help there. He is also very experienced on the national political stage. No Democrat has ever lost Texas and gone on to win a Presidential election.

John Glenn is a Senator from Ohio, whose name has been in the mix for President or Vice President for several years. He originally gained fame as an astronaut in the 1960s, and has fostered a reputation as a moderate Democrat, with a particular interest in science and education. Needless to say, he comes from a crucial state in any national election.

Al Gore has served as a Senator from Tennessee for three years, and like Bush, is the son of a Senator. He has combined a concern for science and technology with a somewhat conservative record on social issues such as gun control, abortion, and gay rights. He did fairly well in the 1988 nomination battle, finishing third to Dukakis and Jesse Jackson. He is also a baby boomer and could help appeal to younger voters.

Jesse Jackson was Dukakis's most successful challenger for the Democratic nomination. He has consistently pushed liberal positions, and would be the first African-American to appear on a major party ticket. In the environment of 1988, his race could be an asset and a liability. Many of supporters feel that his success in the primaries should warrant his selection as the running mate, and passing him up could dampen enthusiasm among black and liberal voters.

fields.description: As expected, Hillary Clinton has carried her party's nomination, and now faces an unexpected opponent in Donald Trump. She was traditionally known as a mainstream Democrat, but tacked significantly to the left during the primary campaign. Clinton enters the general election in a strong position, but she'll be under relentless attack on a number of fronts. Can she make the case that she is truly in touch with the American people -- or that Trump would be an even worse option?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2016 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Donald Trump, you have become the first woman elected to serve as President.

On the political front, it is unclear how much of your agenda you will be able to push forward with the current Congress. Hopefully your victory has helped Democrats further down the ballot. Start packing and prepare to move back into the White House!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

Many of your supporters are despondent that you have faltered to the likes of Donald Trump. Many in the left wing of the party are furious that you pushed their candidate aside, only to lose. Time will tell how Trump operates as President. As for you, a long and sometimes ambiguous political career seems to be coming to its end.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

No candidate secured a majority in the Electoral College. However, the Republicans won a majority in Congress and will elevate Trump to the Presidency. Time will tell how things go in that regard. As for you, a long and sometimes ambiguous political career seems to be coming to its end.

fields.description: Donald Trump has shocked the political establishment by winning the Republican nomination in a divisive contest. He has taken a hard line on immigration and tax cuts, along with unorthodox positions on many other issues. He must unite his own party while finding some way to peel off potential Clinton voters -- or to blunt their enthusiasm for Clinton enough that they stay home. Will he continue the strategy of relentless attack that served him so well in the primary season?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2016 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Hillary Clinton, you have shocked the world with your election victory.

On the political front, you have the bully pulpit in your favor, but both parties in Congress are likely to oppose your next moves, albeit for different reasons. Can you build a working coalition?
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

Many of your supporters are despondent that you have faltered to the likes of Hillary Clinton. Republicans in general believe this was a very winnable election, and are enraged that you came in to blow it. As for your next moves, will you recede quietly from the public spotlight? Or will you do anything you can to case doubt on the legitimacy of the results?
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! You have pulled out 2016 election.

No candidate secured a majority in the Electoral College. However, the Republicans won a majority in Congress and will elevate you to the Presidency. Time will tell how things go in that regard. Any mutual affection between you and Congress is predicted to be short-lived, but you've pulled off a number of surprises to get this far.

fields.description_as_running_mate: Cory Booker is a Senator from New Jersey and was also the Mayor of Newark for several years. Politically, he is a mainstream Democrat, relatively similar to Barack Obama. He is also relatively youthful, with somewhat of a national profile. Turning out the black vote, and preventing even a handful of defectors to Trump, will be essential to a Clinton victory. However, Booker inspires limited enthusiasm amongst Sanders supporters.

Julian Castro is the current Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, under the Obama Administration. He is one of the Democratic Party's highest profile Hispanic politicians, and is a fresh face on the national scene. On the other hand, he is somewhat light on experience, and many argue that Trump's presence will ensure Democratic dominance of the Hispanic vote, regardless of Castro's selection.

Elizabeth Warren is a Senator from Massachusetts and an icon to progressive Democrats. Selecting her could be a good way to appeal to supporters of Bernie Sanders, but she will expect Clinton to adhere to progressive stances throughout the campaign, as a condition of joining the ticket. Some observers think that having two women on the ticket may be a bit much, and also point out that Warren's home state is safely Democratic.

Sherrod Brown is a Senator from Ohio with a long history in that crucial state. He has generally been on the liberal end of the Democratic spectrum, but could help Clinton compete in the Midwest. Brown is reluctant to serve as a running mate this year. Clinton will need to give assurances that her change of position on trade issues, like the Trans-Pacific Partnership, is a permanent change, and was not one of political expediency.

Scott Brown gained national attention for his upset of Martha Coakley in the 2010 Massachusetts Senate race. He was voted out in 2012, and has had trouble gaining political traction in his (admittedly liberal) region, in spite of taking relatively moderate views. Brown has blue-collar bona fides and could help Trump reinforce his anti-establishment image. Geographically, he may provide some measure of help in winning New Hampshire.

Ben Carson was a candidate for President in 2016, with a long history within the evangelical community. He has never served in political office, a fact which may be an asset in this election. Carson was one of the Trump's first opponents to publicly endorse him, and he consistently polled relatively high in the black community during the primary season. However, he has also made a number of bizarre statements and may be vulnerable to a sustained attack campaign.

Chris Christie is the current Governor of New Jersey, and was Trump's first opponent to endorse him, after making his own bid for the Republican nomination. Christie once enjoyed significant bipartisan support in New Jersey, but that has plummeted. His selection would double-down on Trump's image as an unorthodox, East Coast-influenced Republican. This may or may not be helpful.

Ted Cruz was Trump's main rival for the Republican nomination. He is a Senator from Texas who has consistently taken conservative and evangelical positions during his political career. He will only serve as a running mate if Trump makes assurances about his position on the health care issue, federal spending, abortion, and other social issues. He has made it clear that he will withdraw from the ticket if Trump appears to deviate from his promises.

fields.description: Donald Trump has shocked the political establishment by winning the Republican nomination in a divisive contest. He has taken a hard line on immigration and tax cuts, along with unorthodox positions on many other issues. He must unite his own party while finding some way to peel off potential Clinton voters -- or to blunt their enthusiasm for Clinton enough that they stay home. Will he continue the strategy of relentless attack that served him so well in the primary season?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2016 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Hillary Clinton, you have shocked the world with your election victory.

On the political front, you have the bully pulpit in your favor, but support in Congress in uncertain. Will you govern as a more traditional conservative, or will you make a break from orthodoxy?
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

Many of your supporters are despondent that you have faltered to the likes of Hillary Clinton. Republicans in general believe this was a very winnable election, and are enraged that you came in to blow it. Luckily, there are any number of ways for you to take advantage of your newfound exposure. One rumor even has you founding a television station to profit from the aggrieved sensibilities of your followers. The future is in your hands.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! You have pulled out 2016 election.

No candidate secured a majority in the Electoral College. However, the Republicans won a majority in Congress and will elevate you to the Presidency. Time will tell how things go in that regard. Any mutual affection between you and Congress is predicted to be short-lived, but you've pulled off a number of surprises to get this far.

fields.description: As expected, Hillary Clinton has carried her party's nomination, and now faces an unexpected opponent in Donald Trump. She was traditionally known as a mainstream Democrat, but tacked significantly to the left during the primary campaign. Clinton enters the general election in a strong position, but she'll be under relentless attack on a number of fronts. Can she make the case that she truly in touch with the American people -- or that Trump would be an even worse option?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2016 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Donald Trump, you have become the first woman elected to serve as President.

On the political front, it is unclear how much of your agenda you will be able to push forward with the current Congress. Hopefully your victory has helped Democrats further down the ballot. Start packing and prepare to move back into the White House!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

Many of your supporters are despondent that you have faltered to the likes of Donald Trump. Many in the left wing of the party are furious that you pushed their candidate aside, only to lose. Time will tell how Trump operates as President. As for you, a long and sometimes ambiguous political career seems to be coming to its end.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

No candidate secured a majority in the Electoral College. However, the Republicans won a majority in Congress and will elevate Trump to the Presidency. Time will tell how things go in that regard. As for you, a long and sometimes ambiguous political career seems to be coming to its end.

fields.description_as_running_mate: Mike Pence is a former Congressman and the current Governor of Indiana. He is a popular figure among social conservatives and would help assuage concern about Trump among party insiders. He would add executive experience to the ticket and make few mistakes on the campaign trail, but he could also undercut Trump's outsider credentials.

Chris Christie is the current Governor of New Jersey, and was Trump's first opponent to endorse him, after making his own bid for the Republican nomination. Christie once enjoyed significant bipartisan support in New Jersey, but that has plummeted. His selection would double-down on Trump's image as an unorthodox, East Coast-influenced Republican. This may or may not be helpful.

Sarah Palin is the former Governor of Alaska and ill-fated running mate on John McCain's 2008 ticket. Many people believe that she alienated some moderate support and may have cost McCain the election. On the other hand, she endorsed your candidacy relatively early and is still something of a folk hero on the right. In any case, she would certainly help you grab an even greater share of the headlines this fall.

Ben Carson was a candidate for President in 2016, with a long history within the evangelical community. He has never served in political office, a fact which may be an asset in this election. Carson was one of the Trump's first opponents to publicly endorse him, and he consistently polled relatively high in the black community during the primary season. However, he has also made a number of bizarre statements and may be vulnerable to a sustained attack campaign.

Jeff Sessions, a Senator from Alabama, was the first major Republican politician to endorse your candidacy. He could help shore up some potentially shaky support on the right of the Republican party. Conversely, Alabama is not competitive, and sustained attacks on Hillary Clinton may be all that is needed to keep that wing in line.

Tim Kaine has served as a Governor and Senator from Virginia, and shares similar political views to Hillary Clinton. He is fluent in both Spanish and English.

A lot of people see Kaine as a safe, experienced pick. He has little to offer to the wing of the party that supported Bernie Sanders during the nomination fight.

Bernie Sanders was your main opponent in the nomination battle. There's no pretending that the two of you have a warm relationship, but he does have fierce support from many of your potential voters. On the other hand, if you want to make the case that you're a moderate alternative to Trump's extremism, having Bernie on the ticket will not help on that front.

Cory Booker is a Senator from New Jersey and was also the Mayor of Newark for several years. Politically, he is a mainstream Democrat, relatively similar to Barack Obama. He is also relatively youthful, with somewhat of a national profile. Turning out the black vote, and preventing even a handful of defectors to Trump, will be essential to a Clinton victory. However, Booker inspires limited enthusiasm amongst Sanders supporters.

Elizabeth Warren is a Senator from Massachusetts and an icon to progressive Democrats. Selecting her could be a good way to appeal to supporters of Bernie Sanders, but she will expect Clinton to adhere to progressive stances throughout the campaign, as a condition of joining the ticket. Some observers think that having two women on the ticket may be a bit much, and also point out that Warren's home state is safely Democratic.

Sherrod Brown is a Senator from Ohio with a long history in that crucial state. He has generally been on the liberal end of the Democratic spectrum, but could help Clinton compete in the Midwest. Brown is reluctant to serve as a running mate this year. Clinton will need to give assurances that her change of position on trade issues, like the Trans-Pacific Partnership, is a permanent change, and was not one of political expediency.

fields.description: Joe Biden came back from the dead to win the Democratic Party's nomination, and seems to enter the campaign slightly ahead in the polls against incumbent Donald Trump. Emotions are running high, even more than usual, in this campaign. Can Biden live up to his promise to calm tensions, or will he be overwhelmed by events?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2020 election.

Things may have been closer and more contested than you hoped for, but the final result remains. Can you help bring the country back together after a tumultuous few years? Or will you be seen as a lame duck from the first day -- unable to keep the two wings of your party coordinated? Time will tell.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2020 election.

After an election in which many of your supporters claimed democracy itself was at stake, what happens now? Perhaps the party will need to go in a completely different direction in 2024. As for yourself, it seems that your long, illustrious political career has surely drawn to a close.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2020 election.

In spite of the 269-269 tie in the electoral college, Republicans control a majority of state delegations in the House of Representatives. After an election in which many of your supporters claimed democracy itself was at stake, what happens now? Perhaps the party will need to go in a completely different direction in 2024.

fields.description: President Donald Trump enters the campaign with the advantages of incumbency, yet seems to be the underdog for a second time. Can Trump piece together a winning coalition again, and will it be the same one that got him over the finish line in 2016? The pandemic and Black Lives Matter movement only serve to complicate his task even further.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2020 election.

For the second time in a row, many analysts saw a victory for you as practically impossible. But whatever they say, it is clear that your Make America Great Again agenda has been vindicated. Where do you take things from here?
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2020 election.

After an election in which many of your supporters claimed democracy itself was at stake, what happens now? Many analysts believe the party will need to go in a completely different direction next time. As for yourself, will you take these results sitting down, or will you prepare yourself for an epic political comeback in 2024?
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2020 election.

In spite of the 269-269 tie in the electoral college, Republicans control a majority of state delegations in the House of Representatives. A lot of liberals are absolutely distraught and outraged that the election came down to such a technicality, but hey, those are the rules!

fields.description_as_running_mate: Kamala Harris is a Senator from California who made her own run for President in 2020. She would be acceptable to moderates and financial supporters, has some appeal to progressives, and brings diversity to the ticket. She's not the preferred choice of most progressives.

Susan Rice was a UN Ambassador and a National Security Advisor to Barack Obama, and brings decades of foreign policy experience. She would be a true center-left pick, but has never run for elected office. Her foreign policy record would also be a turnoff to progressives.

Karen Bass is a Congresswoman from California and Chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. She has taken more progressive policy stances (including support for Medicare For All) than some of the other candidates, with the attendant supporters and detractors.

Gretchen Whitmer is the Governor of Michigan who could bring some undecideds over the line in that state and region. She is seen as a mainstream Democrat with solid experience. Choosing her would anger some supporters who expect an African-American running-mate after this summer's protests.

Elizabeth Warren is a Senator from Massachusetts who made a serious run at the Democratic Nomination in 2020. She is generally seen as a solid progressive with a particular interest in financial reform and regulation. Choosing her would anger some supporters who expect an African-American running-mate after this summer's protests.

Mike Pence has served as your Vice President for the past four years, sticking to all of your talking points and staying out of the limelight. Most feel he should be rewarded for this loyalty with another turn on the top of the ticket. He also helps shore up your support with social conservatives.

Nikki Haley has served as the Governor of South Carolina, and as a UN Ambassador. She could help you moderate your image and try to close the female vote. Choosing her would probably lead to hard feelings between yourself and Pence, but would your voters care?

Val Demings is a Congresswoman and former police chief from Florida. She could allow Biden to select a black running mate with more moderate credentials than some of the other choices. However, she has had a limited national profile and may be a disappointment to the more progressive wing of the party.

Tammy Duckworth is a Senator from Illinois who served in Iraq and has been active in foreign policy issues. She could help in the Midwest, but was also born in Thailand (as a U.S. citizen) and will need to deflect questions about her eligibility. Additionally, many party activists are expecting an African-American to be selected as well.

fields.description:
Thomas Jefferson is the sitting vice president. The primary author of the Declaration of Independence and leading proponent of democracy and natural rights, Jefferson is considered by many Americans to be the nation’s chief thinker and philosopher.

In 1796, Jefferson narrowly lost the presidency to John Adams after the Federalists castigated him as a dangerous, godless revolutionary and the nation’s “chief Jacobin”. To win, Jefferson will need to manage his reputation from personal attacks while warding off the machinations of Alexander Hamilton, who seeks to manipulate the Election from the shadows.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations, you appear to have won the Election of 1800.

As expected, your party has defeated John Adams and his Federalists. However, it will soon emerge that you have not won outright but, rather, tied among the Electors with Burr. In the subsequent House contingent, Burr will attempt various schemes to steal the presidency which will only be thwarted by the concerted efforts of you, Adams, and—shockingly—Alexander Hamilton. The bitter feelings from this contest will destroy Burr’s credibility among Republicans and indirectly lead to Hamilton’s death four years later.

You will move past all of this. Your decisions on the Louisiana Purchase, the judiciary, the national debt, and more will set the model for the later development of the United States and erase Adams’s vision of a centralized, industrial nation. Your successes will be immortalized while most will choose to forget or ignore your failings on slavery, your personal conduct, your aggressive acquisition of Native lands. Though you will both die on the same day, you will be immortalized as one of America’s greatest presidents while Adams is reduced to a mediocrity. You, not he, shall be remembered as the father of all that transpires over the following 226 years.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the Election of 1800!

Though weighed down by Federalist intrigues, you have suffered a humiliating failure in a contest that many thought skewed in the favor of you and your party. This development is dire for your party and it is also unexpectedly so for John Adams. Instead of being elevated to a second term, the would-be tyrant finds himself outschemed by Alexander Hamilton, tied in Electoral votes with his running mate, Charles Cotesworth Pinckney.

You will reject Adams’s entreaties for support in the contingent, embittered by your loss and determined to retire from politics. Your coalition will help elevate Pinckney and demote Adams to the vice presidency. From Virginia, you will hear fearful developments—of Hamilton handpicking Pinckney’s cabinet, of Hamilton being elevated to commander-in-chief, of a military build-up in anticipation of war with Spain and France. Though many will write seeking advice, you will ignore most of these, trying to content yourself with a life of splendid mediocrity.

At one time, you might have set the mold for this Nation and its development. Instead, you shall be forced to bear witness to the awful fruits of John Adams and his success.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No one has won the Election of 1800!

You have suffered a humiliating failure in a contest many thought skewed in your favor. Your ineptitude in managing both your party and countering Federalist schemes has resulted in no candidate receiving a majority of Elector votes. As outlined in the Constitution, the Election shall now be decided by Congress deciding among the top-five vote recipients.

Adams’s maladministration will be viewed as disqualifying by Federalists and your poor party management viewed similarly by Republicans. Unable to push the Congress to elevate Pinckney, Hamilton will begrudgingly support Monroe over the “unprincipled” Burr—resulting in his election. You will leave politics to manage your estate, but not before castigating Monroe for his coup. He shall achieve little in his term and great dissatisfaction with his leadership shall cause an exodus of many members. By 1816, great disappointment with both parties and an inability to navigate amid hostile powers shall lead Winfield Scott to prevail as a nonpartisan leader. He and Washington will be immortalized as the Fathers of the Nation while you, Adams, and the parties you led descend into obscurity.

fields.description:
John Adams is the sitting President of the United States. A distinguished lawyer, a skilled negotiator, the former vice president, and a major revolutionary thinker, John Adams believes himself the only man qualified for the Executive Mansion.

This inflated sense of self-importance has earned him many enemies. The French Revolution and his fear for what it may represent also has led him to pursue unpopular policies—creating a new “Additional Army”, imposing harsh taxes, and pursuing prosecutions of immigrants and political opponents. These actions have outraged Jeffersonians while doing little to satisfy the allies of Alexander Hamilton, many of whom seek a more malleable vessel for their will.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
You appear to have won the Election of 1800.

Defying every prediction of calamity, you are astonished to find that you have prevailed over popular discontent to win this contest. But the celebrations in Quincy will be fleeting. Soon it will emerge that you have not won outright but instead tied with your running mate, Charles Cotesworth Pinckney. Then the meaning of all of Hamilton’s intrigues will dawn upon you.

Though you will plead and beg, your Federalist compatriots in the Congress will abandon you. An embittered Jefferson will reject your entreaties. You will watch in horror as the House selects Pinckney and forces you back into the role of Vice President. You shall see Hamilton made commander-in-chief, your compromise with the French shredded, the Republican House ignored, the Sedition Acts employed to extremes never dreamt of.

You see all this transpire knowing that it was you and your concessions that made this possible. In thwarting the Jacobins, you midwifed a Napoleon. You, not Jefferson, shall be remembered as the man who delivered all the misfortunes that follow.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the Election of 1800!

As expected the seeds of discontent and division among the Federalists and various internal turmoils have sunk your prospects for the presidency. You will console yourself in your final months by doing all you can to ensure good government— indicating your support for the principled Jefferson over the ambitious Burr in the 1801 contingent election, shepherding a convention with the French through Congress, filling as many posts as you can with Federalists to temper Jefferson’s follies.

You will then return to Quincy for a life of quiet farm work. You will outlive friend and foe alike—Hamilton, Abigail. Your son shall become president and then your name will recede from public memory. At the end of your life, you will come to understand why so many tormented you and accept a world that no longer has need of your ability. On your deathbed, hopeful for this Nation’s future and the democratic spirit which still flows through it, you shall utter one final sentence, “Jefferson lives.”
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No one has won the Election of 1800!

While you have denied Jefferson and his Republicans a majority of votes, various schemes and your own ineptitude in managing Hamilton has resulted in no candidate receiving a majority of Elector votes. As outlined in the Constitution, the Election shall now be decided by Congress deciding among the top-five vote recipients.

You will be cast out as a contender early in this process—too unpopular among all factions. Federalists fearful of an atheistic Jefferson and Republicans fearful of acting president John Marshall shall join together to elevate Aaron Burr as President, believing him to be more easily controlled. Instead, Burr shall reveal himself as an implaccable Republican force, more radical than you believed even Jefferson to be. He shall unwisely expand suffrage, break apart Federalist control of the banks, and undertake a dangerous and costly war with Britain. Sustained by a system of spoils, his popularity among the rabble, and many abuses of the Constitution, he shall serve many ignoble terms. His legacy will outshine both you and Jefferson.

You both shall die on July 4, 1824. One month later, cajoled by Philip Hamilton, New England will attempt secession.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
Charles Cotesworth Pinckney is best known for helping organize South Carolina’s armed resistance to British rule and for helping secure ratification of the federal constitution in South Carolina. He is a successful lawyer and plantation owner who has refused multiple appointments from Washington and Adams. Most recently, Adams attempted to appoint him as an ambassador to France and his subsequent mistreatment nearly precipitated an open war.

Pinckney's presence in this race is an irritant for Adams. Though good-natured and well-liked, he is considered by Adams to be a man of marginal political talents who has been put forward by Hamilton's allies as part of a scheme to exploit federal election rules. Adams worries that Hamilton may try to weaponize Pinckney to keep both Adams and Jefferson out of the Executive Mansion.

In an age where few men are willing to dirty their hands working the room, Aaron Burr has made a name for himself as a campaigner of his considerable talents. His ability to glad-hand with the common man and New York elites alike is unmatched in the young Republic. He is popular in his home of New York City, a former senator and attorney general, and a successful banker.

While he shares Jefferson and Adams’s enmity toward Alexander Hamilton, Burr is viewed with suspicion by both men. He has a reputation for craftiness and intrigue. There are questions about the depths of his commitment to the continued leadership of Jefferson atop the Republican party and to the Republic itself.

At 61, George Clinton is known as the Father of New York. While he had a distinguished military career in both the French and Indian War and the Revolutionary War, Clinton is now best-known as the longest serving governor in the young Republic—with a tenure stretching from 1777 until his retirement in 1795.

Clinton is well-respected in Republican circles, not just for his ardent support of the farmer and yeoman class but for his deep skepticism of federal authority. He opposed the US Constitution and has consistently advocated for states’ rights. His commitments here go further than even Jefferson, whom he distrusts. This combined with his age, general disinterest in campaigning, and refusal to engage in any form of intrigue could make him a difficult partner in politics and government.

fields.description:
Richard Nixon enters the 1968 election with the Republican Party largely united behind him, but struggling with disaffected Independents. With his reputation as a political loser and the stench of Goldwater and Reagan's radicalism, he will have to press the law and order message to win over weary moderates.

Nixon's strong foreign policy experience will likely give him an upper hand on the Vietnam issue, but there are fears that his "secret plan" for an end to the war could create problems down the line. Can Nixon make the case that he's the one who can bring us together again and finally defeat Kennedy?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1968 election.

The liberals will claim they always anticipated this after the chaos in Chicago, but just six years ago they were too busy writing your political obituary to notice the beginning of the greatest comeback since Lazarus. So take some pride in your triumph for now, you've earned it.

On the political front, however, the future is not as rosy. Congress is still in Democratic control, so you'll have a difficult time reining in spending and handling the war. There's also the issue of Bobby Kennedy. There will no doubt be calls for him to run again in 1972 or 1976. So keep an eye out for him. You don't want to be caught sleeping.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1968 election.

There will be plenty of gloating from the liberals about how this was always expected, given your reputation as a political loser, but for a minute there, it really looked like you were on the verge of becoming President of the United States.

This loss is even more painful than it was in 1960, and the added humiliation of losing to a Kennedy brother is lost on no one. Maybe Bobby can secure an honorable exit from Vietnam and reform the current welfare system? In any event, you'll be back in the arena somehow. Whether it's by writing your memoirs, playing the role of elder statesman, or who knows, maybe making one last attempt at reaching the nation's highest office...
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Oh no! We all lost the 1968 election.

This was the outcome everyone had been dreading. After the most divisive year in American history since the Civil War, the country could not agree on who to elect as their next President, effectively ceding all leverage to George Wallace for the next two months, or more.

Riots are already breaking out in the major cities, and the country is battening down the hatches for four more years of unrest and chaos, no matter who comes out of this alive. Who knows, maybe you can put some of those dirty tricks the liberals whine about so much to good use? In any event, it's going to be a bumpy ride.

fields.description:
Robert F. Kennedy faces the difficult task of uniting the Democratic Party at a time when it seems to be tearing at the seams. His shocking challenge to President Johnson and even more unprecedented victory in Chicago may have electrified the nation's youth and minorities, but there are questions about whether his liberal politics can win over the hardhat vote.

Can Kennedy's brand of "New Politics" craft a new political coalition from the ashes of the tried and true Democratic one his brother held together eight years ago?
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1968 election.

After the Chicago riots, you looked like a goner, but it seems the American people had other thoughts. Your supporters are ecstatic and the Kennedy family begins preparing to move back into the White House like nothing ever happened.

But you've got much bigger problems to deal with. Vietnam is the most obvious, but the deteriorating conditions of the cities, the moral crisis of rural poverty, and still-widespread inequality will make things all the more difficult. That's not even to mention the economic warnings signs blinking red. But who knows, maybe you can weather the storm and make it through to a second term?
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1968 election.

Perhaps your campaign was always doomed after the chaos of Chicago, but you really thought you had a chance there. Your supporters are despondent at the prospect of a Nixon administration, and the party is more divided than ever over what direction to go in next. McCarthy and Johnson are no doubt crowing about your defeat right now.

You still maintain a strong base of support among liberals and minorities however, and who knows what state the country will be in after four years of Nixon. Hopefully he'll find a way to pull out of Vietnam and rein in government spending, but if not, maybe you could give it another shot? You are only 42 after all.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Oh no! We all lost the 1968 election.

This was the national nightmare everyone had been dreading. Now that it has come to pass, Wallace is already riling up his supporters by promising them nothing less than the abolition of every civil rights law on the books. Riots are breaking out in major cities and there are whispers that Johnson's going to send in the Army within the next 24 hours to quell the uprisings.

Meanwhile there's still the drama to play out in the House, where Democrats currently hold a majority. But don't get too comfortable, many within your party still haven't warmed up to your unabashed liberal idealism, to say nothing of whatever offers Wallace is throwing their way, or Nixon's pleas for unity. So fasten your seatbelts, it's going to be a bumpy ride.

fields.description:
George Wallace is the segregationist Governor of Alabama and the face of the anti-integration movement in the United States. The recent death of his wife, Lurleen, and widespread allegations of corruption in office may make his hopeless run even more complicated.

A hero in the South, Wallace is running an openly racist third party campaign competing in all 50 states. With no chances of winning outright, Wallace hopes to deadlock the electoral college and strong-arm the ultimate winner into repealing civil rights legislation.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2000 election.

This was definitely not supposed to happen. Good luck!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
As expected, you have lost the 2000 election.

The legacy of this campaign depends on a couple of factors. First of all, did you receive 5% of the popular vote? If so, congratulations! You will enable the Green Party to run a vigorous campaign in 2004 and present a true choice to the American people. Also, the Democrats were a little peeved that you "stole" votes from them in this election. Hopefully that doesn't lead to a backlash.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! No candidate received 270 electoral votes, but the House will elect George W. Bush as President.

Did you receive 5% of the popular vote? If so, congratulations! You will enable the Green Party to run a vigorous campaign in 2004 and present a true choice to the American people. Also, the Democrats were a little peeved that you "stole" votes from them in this election. Hopefully that doesn't lead to a backlash, especially since they will lose the vote in the House.

fields.description_as_running_mate: Howard Baker is the son-in-law of Everett Dirksen. He is also the newly elected Senator from Tennessee. Part of the Republican wave of 1966, Baker's moderation would placate northerners and liberals while probably keeping southern Republicans in line. Strom Thurmond has stated he would not oppose Baker's selection.

Chuck Percy is a popular and recently elected Republican from Illinois. A rising star since the Eisenhower administration, Percy is well-respected within the party establishment. His endorsement of Nelson Rockefeller angered the Nixon camp however. Percy's selection would also surely upset the Southern wing, likely increasing Wallace's support, but he could potentially offset it in northern cities with his focus on urban affairs.

John Lindsay is the Mayor of New York City. As a staunchly liberal Republican, Lindsay would appeal to minorities and potentially win over some of Kennedy's base. His stances on civil rights and other key social issues will likely turn off Southern conservatives however. Lindsay's height and good looks might gain the Nixon campaign some critical youth support though, and he will certainly garner favorable media coverage.

Spiro Agnew is the second-year Governor of Maryland. A supporter of Rockefeller, Agnew had a strong civil rights record until changing his tune in the wake of an increasingly militant movement and riots in 1967. His appeal to white backlash could make Nixon's attempts to win favor among black Republicans difficult. There are also corruption concerns.

Harold Hughes is the third term Governor of Iowa. Wildly popular in his home state, Hughes has little name recognition to most voters. Hughes could go a long way toward winning back Kennedy some of the farm vote from the Nebraska primary, but there are concerns about his readiness for the job. Hughes is beloved by his liberal colleagues despite his penchant for making strange statements to the press.

Warren Hearnes is the first term Governor of Missouri. His challenge to the remnants of the Pendergast machine endeared him to anti-machine New Politics liberals. His selection would go over well in the border states and Midwest. But his self-promotion and support for the Johnson line on Vietnam could pose a problem.

John McKeithen is the segregationist Governor of Louisiana. McKeithen's close relationship with the Ku Klux Klan and other white supremacist groups in his state would undoubtedly complicate his selection. There are also still unverified charges of his ties to New Orleans racketeers. McKeithen would immediately strengthen Kennedy's support in the South, but weaken him everywhere else.

Hubert Humphrey has served as Vice President of the United States under Lyndon Johnson following their landslide election in 1964. His tenure has been tumultuous, with civil rights initiatives and the war in Vietnam roiling the party. Humphrey's selection would be seen as a sop to the very establishment Kennedy launched his campaign against and would likely turn away much of his core base. But Humphrey's strength with the badly-needed labor vote is undeniable.

Ezra Taft Benson was President Eisenhower's Secretary of Agriculture. As a devout Mormon Benson could strengthen Wallace's odds out West while keeping the South in check due to his racist beliefs. Benson's anticommunist image has gained him support from the John Birch Society and other right-wing groups, but his isolationist leanings could complicate that.

But Wallace is running out of time and money. At this rate, it'll be a miracle if he has a running mate by November at all, and he'll certainly miss the filing deadlines in a number of states. That is, if anyone will say yes to him.

Curtis LeMay is a General and the former Air Force Chief of Staff who served during the Second World War and is considered a hero of the Berlin Airlift. A known critic of the Kennedy and Johnson policy on Vietnam, he will certainly add a hawkish undertone to the campaign, though some fear that may be a negative, even for Wallace.

But Wallace is running out of time and money. At this rate, it'll be a miracle if he has a running mate by November at all, and he'll certainly miss the filing deadlines in a number of states. That is, if anyone will say yes to him.

fields.description: Candidate description here.

Theodore Roosevelt runs as the Republican nominee after years of agitating for war and attacking Wilson's leadership. Once the champion of progressive reform, he has abandoned that cause almost entirely in favor of nationalism, the protective tariff, and hostility to hyphenated Americans.

Roosevelt is the favorite, but the war is unpopular and his attacks on hyphenated Americans have alienated large immigrant communities. His own health has also declined since his last run. He must make the case that only he can bring the war to a victorious conclusion.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1920 election.

After years of agitating for war and attacking Wilson's leadership, you have won the Presidency for a second time. The crowds that throng the streets of New York are enormous, and you can barely contain yourself as you address your loyal supporters.

On the political front, the war will now be prosecuted to its fullest extent. The League of Nations is dead, the protective tariff is secure, and the era of 100% Americanism has begun. Whether the country can survive another year of war, and whether your health can survive the Presidency, remain open questions.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1920 election.

Despite your best efforts, the American people have rejected your candidacy. The war weariness that you dismissed as cowardice proved to be something deeper, and your attacks on hyphenated Americans alienated more voters than they inspired.

You return to Sagamore Hill in declining health, with the knowledge that the great cause of your life has been repudiated at the ballot box. The Republican Party will need to find a new standard-bearer. With the progressive wing you once led now scattered to the winds, word is that Philander Knox is the favorite for 1924.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No candidate has captured an Electoral College majority.

For the first time since 1824, no candidate has won a majority of the electoral votes. The election will be decided by the House of Representatives, where each state delegation casts a single vote.

The Republicans control a majority of state delegations, and after frantic negotiations, they deliver the Presidency to Theodore Roosevelt. It is not the mandate you wanted, but you have the office, and you intend to use it. Debs's handful of electoral votes are irrelevant in the House, where Socialist representation is negligible, but his supporters are staging mass demonstrations outside the Capitol demanding that the will of the people be respected. The country enters 1921 more divided than at any point since the Civil War. Good luck!

fields.description:
Woodrow Wilson seeks an unprecedented third term after a severe stroke has left him partially incapacitated. The true extent of his condition is a closely guarded secret. The war he promised to end drags on, and the crackdowns under the Espionage Act have outraged progressives and immigrants alike.

Roosevelt's nativist campaign has made Wilson, almost by accident, the champion of immigrant voters, for better or worse. He must defend the war, promote his League of Nations, and convince the public he is fit to serve.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1920 election.

Against all expectations, you have won an unprecedented third term. Your progressive legacy is secure, and the League of Nations has been given a second life.

On the political front, the true extent of your illness remains a secret. The war drags on, the economy is strained, and the Senate remains hostile to your League. You have four more years, but the question of whether you are truly fit to serve them will not go away. Your legacy now depends on ending this war and securing the peace you have promised the world.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1920 election.

The American people have spoken, and they have had enough. The war you promised to end drags on, the crackdowns under the Espionage Act have outraged the very progressives you needed, and the rumors about your health have taken their toll.

You leave the White House diminished in body and reputation. The League of Nations, your life's work, will almost certainly die in the Senate without a sympathetic President to champion it. Prepare to join Grant, and ironically, Roosevelt as Presidents denied their third term.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No candidate has captured an Electoral College majority.

For the first time since 1824, no candidate has won a majority of the electoral votes. The election will be decided by the House of Representatives, where each state delegation casts a single vote.

The Republicans control a majority of state delegations, and despite your showing, they will deliver the Presidency to Theodore Roosevelt. Your supporters are outraged, and the Socialists are using this opportunity to stage mass demonstrations in favor of a general strike to end the war. You return to private life a broken man, and the League of Nations dies with your Presidency.

fields.description:
Eugene Debs is running for President from Cell 2253 of a federal penitentiary in Atlanta, where he is serving a ten-year sentence for opposing the draft. He is the most famous political prisoner in the country, and his candidacy is as much a protest against wartime repression as it is a bid for office. The Socialist Party has nominated him unanimously.

Debs has no realistic path to the Presidency, but a strong showing could establish the Socialists as a permanent force in American politics. Every speech must be delivered by surrogates or by written statement from his cell.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1920 election.

From Cell 2253 of a federal penitentiary in Atlanta, Eugene V. Debs has been elected President of the United States. Nothing like this has ever happened in the history of the republic, and nothing like it is likely to happen again.

The political establishment is in a state of complete panic. Wall Street is in freefall, the major parties are in disarray, and the question of whether a prisoner can legally assume the Presidency is being debated in every courtroom and newspaper editorial page in the country. One thing is certain--the working people of America have sent a message that can never be taken back.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1920 election.

You were never expected to win, and you did not. But the campaign was never really about winning. It was about proving that the Socialist movement could survive the Espionage Act, the Palmer raids, and the imprisonment of its leader.

You remain in your cell in Atlanta, but your vote total will be studied carefully by both major parties and historians to come. If the Socialists can hold this coalition together, they may yet become a permanent force in American politics. For now, you write letters, receive visitors, and wait for the pardon that may or may not come.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
No candidate has captured an Electoral College majority.

For the first time since 1824, no candidate has won a majority of the electoral votes. The election will be decided by the House of Representatives, where each state delegation casts a single vote.

There is no scenario in which the House selects a Socialist prisoner as President. The delegations will choose between Roosevelt and Wilson, and you will remain in your cell regardless of the outcome. But the fact that Eugene Debs threw the election into the House from a federal penitentiary is a story that will be told for generations. A new era has arrived, and everyone knows it.

fields.description_as_running_mate: Thomas Marshall has served as Wilson's Vice President since 1913. The two have never been close, but Marshall is popular in Indiana and inoffensive everywhere else. Keeping him on the ticket avoids a distracting storyline and preserves party unity. He adds nothing in the way of excitement or energy to a campaign that could badly use both.

A. Mitchell Palmer is the Attorney General and the architect of the government's crackdown on radicals, anarchists, and suspected Communists. He is from Pennsylvania, a state Wilson badly needs. His selection would shore up the law-and-order vote, but his raids on immigrant communities have made him a villain to exactly the voters that Roosevelt's nativism is driving into Wilson's arms.

Al Smith is the Governor of New York, a Tammany man, a Catholic, and a wet. In other words, he is everything that appeals to the urban immigrant voter, while driving away rural Protestant America in equal measure. His selection would energize the cities and lock down New York, but it would cause real problems in the South and the dry states. Wilson's personal feelings about Tammany Hall are well known.

Albert Fall is a Senator from New Mexico and one of Roosevelt's closest allies in Congress. He is a hard-line conservative on every issue—pro-war, pro-business, anti-labor, and anti-immigration. Roosevelt has called him the embodiment of the best American Spirit. His selection would complete the merger of the New Nationalists with the Republican old guard, but would make it very difficult to win back any progressive voters who are drifting toward Wilson or even Debs.

Albert Beveridge is the chairman of the Republican National Committee, a former Senator from Indiana and one of Roosevelt's oldest allies. He made his name fighting for the Meat Inspection Act and child labor laws, but his politics were always grounded in a fierce Anglo-Saxon nationalism. Since 1914 the reformism has fallen away entirely. He is now an opponent of the income tax, a critic of organized labor, and a leading voice for immigration restriction. His Indiana roots and role as party chairman could help in the Midwest, but he will do little to win back progressives who have already written Roosevelt off.

Hiram Johnson is the Governor of California and Roosevelt's running mate from the 1912 Progressive ticket. He is the last credible link to the old reform movement, and his selection could hold some progressive voters in the West who might otherwise drift to Debs. Johnson had voted to join the Great War in 1917, but has grown skeptical since, and it is not clear that he and Roosevelt still see eye to eye on the biggest issue of the campaign.

Seymour Stedman is a Chicago lawyer and longtime Socialist Party official. He is the respectable face of the movement—articulate, well-dressed, and capable of making the party's case to middle-class progressives without frightening them. With Debs in prison, the running mate will be doing most of the actual campaigning, and Stedman is the safest pair of hands available.

Kate Richards O'Hare was recently released from prison after serving time under the Espionage Act for an anti-war speech in North Dakota. Her selection would put two political prisoners on the same ticket and make government repression the central issue of the campaign. She would also be the first woman on a national ticket.

John Reed is a journalist and revolutionary who witnessed the Bolshevik Revolution firsthand and wrote Ten Days That Shook the World. He is young, charismatic, and famous, and his selection would mend fences with the party's schismatic left wing. He is also a Communist sympathizer, which will be used against the Socialist ticket every single day of the campaign by both major parties.

fields.description:
FDR has served as New York Governor since 1929. He comes from two storied families—the Delanos and the Roosevelts—and had known a life of unthinkable privilege until his sudden debilitating battle with polio. Losing the use of his legs, this hardship has solidified a resolve in Roosevelt that government aid to the needy is a matter of social duty, not mere charity.

As Governor of the largest state, Roosevelt built on his decades of political contacts—dating back to his time in the Navy Department during the Great War and his tutelage under Al Smith—to assemble a juggernaut of a presidential campaign. With one eye on the presidency, FDR views his vast public works programs and economic relief in the Empire State as the forerunner of his even more ambitious national plans.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Happy Days Are Here Again!

With a third of the nation unemployed and a sense of fear pervading the country akin to the Dark Ages, perhaps the odds were always in your favor. But don't kid yourself, things could have gone wrong at any moment. Shortly after your triumph, they nearly would in Miami, where a crazed gunman will barely miss you, and claim the life of the mayor.

You have triumphed over polio, over depression, and now even over death itself. Yet nothing can prepare you for the hard times ahead. In-between the election and your inauguration, the banking system is pushed past the breaking point, bringing the nation to a terrifying halt. As you stare outside the window on the train to Washington, the enormity of the crisis at hand weighs heavy on the heart.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1932 Presidential Election.

To say this comes as a blow would be a gross understatement. With the nation facing its worst financial calamity in history, how could you fail to unseat Herbert Hoover? Democrats won't waste a moment engaging in finger-pointing after their divisive convention this Summer.

Unfortunately for you, seeing as your nomination was already a difficult feat, it seems your political career is at an end. Perhaps you can retire to Warm Springs and work on your polio foundation there. It would be a noble legacy.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Fear Itself.

The Great Depression is the greatest crisis this nation has stared down since the Civil War, and now it too may end in one. With the banking system in tatters and the societal fabric of the nation tearing apart, even American democracy itself is in doubt. There is no saying what happens now. As the House prepares to vote, the simmering rage which swept the country these past three years reaches a boiling point.

fields.description:
Herbert Hoover is the unpopular incumbent President of the United States. Elected in a landslide in 1928 against FDR's mentor, Hoover's improbable rags-to-riches story at one time made him the most beloved man in America. Raised in a shack in West Branch, Iowa, and embarking on a lifetime of ingenuity taking him to China during the Boxer Rebellion and war-ravaged Europe in the throes of famine, it was inevitable that one day Hoover would land in the White House.

But the economic crash of 1929 ended all hopes of another four years of business-as-usual Republican governance, and Hoover's perceived inaction has all-but-fatally doomed his presidency. Worse yet, the major programs Hoover has to his name have worsened the crisis in the eyes of millions. It will take Heaven and Earth for Hoover to prove to the American people that he still has what it takes to lead.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Wow! You have won the 1932 Presidential Election.

After you glided to the presidency just four short years ago, few could have anticipated the endurance test your term would turn out to be. But those who knew you and your life story best never wavered. The American people have placed their confidence in you once again. Perhaps they felt your ambitious public works projects and the RFC were beginning to turn things around?
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1932 Presidential Election.

This comes as a bitter pill to swallow, but after seeing the anger roiling the country in these final weeks, it is an expected one. Few men have as many stunning accomplishments and failures as you. But there is no time to wallow in your misery. Amidst the four-month long transition to Roosevelt, the already wobbling banking system is now on the brink of collapse. The hardest times are yet to come.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Fear Itself

In these angry days, it is anyone’s guess what happens now. Riots are already breaking out in Washington, with an angry mob gathering outside the White House. There’s no MacArthur to save you now. Hunker down and pray that you, and the country, can make it through these next four months alive. They will be the hardest any American will ever experience.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
John Garner is a Texas Congressman and Speaker of the House. A 19th century pork-barrel politician, Garner is known for his heavy-handed maneuvering on the Hill and a harsh temper. Presiding over a three-vote majority in the chamber, Garner has sought to work with Hoover on fiscal matters, particularly balancing the budget, even if it means unpopular tax increases.

Most importantly, Garner's selection would swing the Texas delegation behind FDR at the Democratic Convention, making his path to the nomination easier.

Albert Ritchie is the four-term Governor of Maryland. A highly experienced politician, Ritchie has been angling for the presidency himself this year, but now appears likely to throw the Maryland delegation behind Newton Baker in the event of a deadlock.

Courtly and conservative, Ritchie would please southerners in the party, even if the newspapers ridicule his lack of name recognition nationally. But his callous rhetoric towards the unemployed in his state may rub voters the wrong way, remarking that “I do not know where you get the idea that anybody is starving in this state, no such conditions exist here.”

Newton Baker is the former Secretary of War. A proud Wilsonian internationalist, Baker rubs isolationists and anti-imperialists in the party the wrong way, and may ignite the largely dormant Bryan faction, including William Randolph Hearst.

Since leaving government, Baker has worked as an attorney for utility companies, endearing himself to big business and military veterans. Baker is widely regarded as an attractive compromise candidate, should the convention deadlock.

William Gibbs McAdoo is the former Secretary of the Treasury and the late President Wilson’s son-in-law. Having run for president twice himself, in 1920 and 1924, some in the party view McAdoo as yesterday’s man, but he still commands a large following in the all-important California delegation.

A lifelong “dry” on the Prohibition issue, McAdoo has signaled that he’s willing to change his mind if the party reaches a “wet” consensus. More alarming is his open courting of the Klan vote back in 1924, which could jeopardize Roosevelt’s support among northern blacks this Fall.

Charles Curtis is the sitting Vice President of the United States. At age seventy-three, there is a growing party consensus that Curtis does not have the stamina to serve another four years. But if Hoover is to have any chance at re-election, it will have to be with a unified party behind him. A bitter nominating contest over the running mate slot would all but doom him.

Popular in the farm states, Curtis is a conservative Republican and the first Native American Vice President in history. He has been a loyal soldier for your administration, often casting tie-breaking votes in the Senate after 1930 midterm defeats. Curtis’ sister, Dolly, however, has become a running joke in Washington social circles for her extravagant parties amidst financial ruin nationally.

Charles Dawes is the former Vice President of the United States and present Ambassador to the United Kingdom. An influential figure in diplomatic circles, Dawes is a traditional internationalist pro-business Republican. His association with the Coolidge years may help or hurt, depending on whether Hoover intends to run a conservative campaign or not.

There are additional concerns about dropping the incumbent Vice President in the midst of a bitter contest.

Hiram Johnson is a maverick Senator from California and one of the most prominent progressives in the country. Johnson’s selection would send shockwaves through the Republican Party, after he bolted the GOP to run on Theodore Roosevelt’s “Bull Moose” ticket in 1912. But if he is not selected, Johnson is threatening to endorse FDR instead.

There are additional concerns about dropping the incumbent Vice President in the midst of a bitter contest.

fields.description:
