Despite his loss four years prior, Grover Cleveland has been renominated by the Democrats and is expected to win the election against Benjamin Harrison.

Recent Democratic gains in much of the Midwest gives the former President much reason to be confident in his ability to win. The large amounts of spending by Congress plays well into Cleveland's message of responsible finance and clean, honest government. Cleveland can focus on attacking Harrison against his own record, or attempt to win back support out west by moderating on his monetary stances.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2000 election.

Though it was perhaps expected, you could have easily faltered at a number of points. Credit to you for pulling through.

On the political front, you can continue the Clinton legacy and strengthen Social Security for generations to come. Perhaps you can succeed on health care where Clinton came up short? Or maybe you can create a future of renewable energy for America. Just be wary of a (George or Jeb?) Bush challenge in 2004.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2000 election.

Surely the second-guessing will be intense, but if things were close you could probably run again in 2004.

It seems that with George W. Bush and a Republican majority, the United States can expect some conservative policy-making over the next four years. Hopefully Bush comes through on his promise to govern in a bipartisan, conciliatory manner. A lot should depend on the margin of his victory, and whether it was large or small.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost in a squeaker.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, for the first time since 1824. Unfortunately for you, a majority of states have Republican controlled congressional delegations.

It seems that with George W. Bush and a Republican majority, the United States can expect some conservative policy-making over the next four years. Hopefully Bush comes through on his promise to govern in a bipartisan, conciliatory manner.

fields.description:
President Benjamin Harrison enters the 1892 campaign facing several headwinds. Elected in 1888 while losing the "popular vote" to Cleveland, Harrison has struggled to enact much of his agenda, most notably a failed voting rights law.

Initially opposed to running, Harrison has only pressed forth to oppose James Blaine's attempts to secure the nomination for himself. Harrison hopes to win enough of the Midwest by defending the so-called "McKinley tariffs" passed in 1890. He could also stake the campaign on the failed voting rights law blocked by the Senate.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2000 election.

Confounding the predictions of many experts, you were able to turn the tables on Al Gore, in spite of the economy and Clinton's popularity.

On the political front, you can push for tax cuts to spur the economy and return the budget surplus to the American people. You might also pursue education and immigration reform, individual Social Security accounts, and new laws to defend the family and the sanctity of life.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2000 election.

Perhaps it was always a long-shot, with the Democrats in such a commanding position after eight years of Bill Clinton. In any case, at least you are still the Governor of Texas.

Expect Al Gore to unleash a new round of government programs and environmental regulations. You are still youngish, however. If the election was close this time, perhaps you can run again in 2004, or work on behalf your brother Jeb.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! You have won in a squeaker.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, marking the first time this has happened since 1824. Fortunately for you, the majority of U.S. states have Republican controlled congressional delegations, and they will cast their votes accordingly.

Given the incredibly close nature of the election, you will surely be expected to govern as a moderate, conciliatory President. Right??

fields.description:
The emerging Populist Party, following success in the 1890 elections, has nominated James Weaver, a former Congressman from Iowa.

Weaver starts out in a solid position out in the Western states, where his stance in favor of the unlimited coinage of silver has much support amongst members of both parties. However, the Populists hope to compete in the former Confederacy, which might bring problems for Weaver given his Union service in the Civil War.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2000 election.

This was definitely not supposed to happen. Good luck!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
As expected, you have lost the 2000 election.

The legacy of this campaign depends on a couple of factors. First of all, did you receive 5% of the popular vote? If so, congratulations! You will enable the Green Party to run a vigorous campaign in 2004 and present a true choice to the American people. Also, the Democrats were a little peeved that you "stole" votes from them in this election. Hopefully that doesn't lead to a backlash.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! No candidate received 270 electoral votes, but the House will elect George W. Bush as President.

Did you receive 5% of the popular vote? If so, congratulations! You will enable the Green Party to run a vigorous campaign in 2004 and present a true choice to the American people. Also, the Democrats were a little peeved that you "stole" votes from them in this election. Hopefully that doesn't lead to a backlash, especially since they will lose the vote in the House.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
Whitelaw Reid is a diplomat and publisher who has long held ties to the Republican Party. With Morton being dropped from the ticket, Reid is the safe and standard choice to be Harrison's running mate, given his ability to run a vigorous campaign.

It should be noted that Reid does hold some conservative views on business, which could agitate and push away the growing Populist movement.

William McKinley is the Governor of Ohio, and was previously a Congressman before being turned around in the 1890 Democratic rout. He is, of course, also the namesake of the McKinley tariff, which he helped draft.

By selecting him, the Republican Party would be aggressively staking their support on the tariff issue. McKinley's personal ambition may also get in the way, as he attempted to position himself as a candidate at the 1892 convention.

Henry Lodge is a Congressman from Massachusetts, most well known for drafting the Federal Elections Bill, known by supporters as the ''Lodge Bill'' and detractors as the ''Force Bill''. Still, Lodge is relatively young and would be capable of running an energetic campaign against the Democrats and Populists.

If nominated to be Harrison's running mate, the voting rights law would be one of the top issues of the campaign, which may help or hurt depending on Harrison's strategy.

Adlai Stevenson is the former assistant Postmaster General and Congressman. He is from Illinois, a crucial and large state that Cleveland hopes to win, and he may help keep the South in line due to his opposition on the so-called ''Force Bill''.

However, Stevenson is pro-Silver, something Cleveland would have to deal with, or attempt to use to his advantage.

Henry Watterson is a former Congressman and journalist from Kentucky. He could help keep the south in line at a time when several states are at risk of bolting to the Populists. His journalism background could also help him communicate with the public.

It should be noted that Watterson was also a Confederate soldier. If he is nominated, Republicans will surely wave the bloody shirt against Cleveland.

Horace Boies is the Governor of Iowa, a state that was expected to go for Harrison but could be in play if Boies is added to the ticket. Boies is a strong supporter of low tariffs, an issue that the campaign will be fought on.

For better or for worse, Boies would appeal greatly to the western factions of the party, due to his strong support of free silver, something Cleveland will have to address.

James Field is a Populist figure from Virginia, previously serving as the state's Attorney General many years prior. As a former Confederate General, Field would help Weaver compete in the south.

However, Field has been out of elected politics for quite some time, and it is unknown if he will have the vigor to aggressively campaign.

Thomas Watson is a sitting Congressman from Georgia, elected on the Democratic ticket. As a running mate, Watson would hopefully give the Populists a strong chance at winning multiple states.

It should be noted that Watson does have some views on voting rights that would be controversial in the South, but overall he should be a net benefit in this region.

Edward Bellamy is an author from Massachusetts and has labored for the Populist cause for some time. His writing skills could absolutely be a benefit to the campaign.

Many of Bellamy's views are radical and outright socialistic in nature, something which the party's opponents will take advantage of if not handled carefully.

fields.description:
Returning to the presidential stage after a nail-biter defeat to Gerald Ford in the 1976 Republican primaries, Ronald Reagan overcame a formidable field to seize the nomination this year. With Jimmy Carter infuriating liberal Democrats and Republican hardliners alike, the ground seems fertile for the kind of conservative revolution Reagan's ideological heirs have always dreamed of.

But the California Governor faces serious doubts about his ability to lead, with loose lips and a gaffe-prone campaign leading many to believe he's just a dim Hollywood actor after all.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1980 election!

With your victory, you have ushered in a new era of American politics, realigning the country around your conservative principles and shattering the old Democratic coalition. For the first time since the 1920's, the dominant party is the GOP. Now your job is to make it last.

On the domestic front, your top priority will be getting the country out of the recession. Whether your massive tax and spending cuts will make the difference is unclear. The global situation is even more tenuous. You face a resurgent Soviet threat in Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and of course, the 52 American hostages still remaining in Iran. Will they still be there when you take the Oath of Office?
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1980 election.

After such a euphoric convention, this loss is a devastating one for the conservative movement to take. The finger-pointing is sure to drag on for months, perhaps years. With double-digit inflation and Americans languishing in Iran, everyone thought you were a sure thing.

At your advanced age, this is an end to a long and unsuccessful entry into politics. With your mixed record as California governor, Gerald Ford's chief critic before his defeat in 1976, and now the man who lost to Jimmy Carter, your legacy is likely to be nil to all but the most ardent National Review readers. Perhaps you can go back to Hollywood?
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! No candidate holds a majority in the electoral college.

Anderson's third party candidacy has succeeded beyond his own supporters' wildest expectations. What happens next is anyone's guess.

Anderson does not hold enough of an electoral bloc in Congress to become president himself, but will the institution which Carter has routinely denigrated for four years elevate him for another term? Or will the Democratic majority elect a radical right-winger? Either way, get used to the phrase “President Tip O’Neill.”

fields.description:
It seems like a lifetime ago when Jimmy Carter entered the White House with his approval rating in the stratosphere. After Watergate and Vietnam, Americans were ready for an end to the divisions and national traumas of the last decade, but all they got was more of the same. Plagued by economic downturns and a Cold War turning hot, Carter's reelection prospects look bleak.

A brutal intra-party fight has hardly helped the Democrats' odds this November. Ted Kennedy's campaign may have gone down in flames, but he remains an icon to millions of voters Jimmy Carter must win over if he is to have any hope of staying in the White House another four years.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1980 election!

Your reelection appeared hopeless for most of the campaign, but it appears enough voters felt they were better off with the devil they know.

Of course, now you have to actually act on the ambitious domestic programs you promised to alleviate the ongoing recession. That will be easier said than done with a Congress tilting heavily to the right.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1980 election.

In 1976 you promised to never tell a lie, so you can't say it doesn't hurt. But after the crisis of confidence this nation has suffered in the 1970s, it's not surprising that you have become the fifth straight president who failed to serve two full terms.

Reagan's victory appears to be a realigning moment for the two major parties, both of which are now lurching rightward. In the meantime, you'll have to busy yourself with ongoing hostage negotiations before you leave office. After that, who knows? You'll probably just return to Plains and open a stuffy library.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Oh no! No candidate holds a majority in the electoral college.

You had been dreading this outcome all along. It seems Anderson was a far greater force to be reckoned with than anyone thought.

After you've alienated so many of the same congressional liberals now flocking to Anderson, it seems unlikely you'll be able to pull through. But who knows? You've made it this far...

fields.description:
Illinois Congressman John Anderson runs as a third-party candidate, hoping to cobble together enough Kennedy Democrats and moderate Republicans to break through the noise in November. While he is still an unknown to many, if Anderson's polls remain high—some surveys have him above 30%—his record in the House will surely be called into question.

Anderson's goal of winning outright is unrealistic, if not impossible. He will have to deflect accusations of acting as a "spoiler" for Reagan and the Republicans, or Carter and the Democrats, depending on who's talking. But there is an outside shot that Anderson may deadlock the race and throw it to the House, in which case, all bets are off.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Wow! You have won the 1968 election in a shocker!

Dixie forever! Even with the Long Hot Summer of 1967, nobody guessed that you could do well enough in the Northern states to win the election outright. You have instantly become most polarizing President-elect since Abraham Lincoln.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you did not prevent an electoral college majority.

You put in a good effort, but your dream of brokering an end to desegregation will not come to fruition in 1968. No winning candidate will negotiate that point with you unless they absolutely have no choice.

The best you can do for now is continue to sound the call for a return to sanity in American politics. Perhaps if the riots and discord continue, you will have a better chance of making your voice heard in 1972.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Congratulations! You have deadlocked the electoral college with your votes in the South.

In a close election, your electoral votes in the South have prevented either candidate from winning a majority. Get ready to put the squeeze on Humphrey and Nixon.

Of course, you still have to deal with the possibility that Humphrey and Nixon dislike you so much that they will simply strike a deal with each other. Whatever happens, it's sure to be interesting.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
George Bush is the former CIA Director and Ambassador to China. His years of experience in Republican politics paid off with his 1980 presidential campaign. Bush's upset victory in Iowa forced Reagan to take the Bonesman seriously and reckon with this Ivy League WASP's unique appeal to black voters and liberal Republicans.

That same support from minorities and internationalists is now jeopardizing Bush's vice presidential bid, with Jesse Helms threatening to walk out of the Republican convention if Reagan were to select Bush.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Gerald Ford is the former President of the United States and the man who beat Ronald Reagan four years ago. It would be unprecedented for Ford to be tapped as Reagan's running mate for those same reasons. But the former president has been making the rounds on the three networks, selling himself as a "co-president," who would handle foreign policy while Reagan sat at the kids table.

It is an open question whether that would be an asset for the ticket or not.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Jack Kemp is a Republican Congressman from New York and former NFL player. With his good looks and telegenic appeal, Kemp openly draws comparisons to John F. Kennedy. But his staunch supply-side economic views have led some moderates in the Republican Party to believe Kemp is more of a radical than he lets on.

Of course, that unshakeable conservative ideology could work to Reagan's favor in certain regions of the country. It would certainly end any outlandish talk of a protest bid from the radical right faction, but were they ever going to go through with that anyway?

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Howard Baker is a Republican Senator from Tennessee. The son-in-law of Everett Dirksen, Baker endeared himself to the GOP Old Guard with his tough questioning of Nixon administration officials during the Watergate hearings. A proud moderate, Baker would boost Reagan's odds in New England, but could rock the boat with ultra-conservatives like Dan Crane and Jesse Helms.

Gerald Ford nearly selected Baker as his own running mate in 1976, until Baker revealed to the president that his wife, Joy, was a recovering alcoholic. Ford chose Bob Dole instead and lost.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Walter Mondale is Vice President of the United States and a former Senator from Minnesota. A strong ally of liberal icon Hubert Humphrey, Mondale is a classical New Dealer, supporting expensive social welfare legislation, even when it clashes with Jimmy Carter's own beliefs.

Because of these disagreements, Mondale has had doubts about remaining on the ticket this year. But after the challenge from Kennedy, it would be unwise for the president to sever his closest tie to the liberal wing of the party before the election.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Jerry Brown is the Governor of California and a two-time presidential candidate. While his long-shot bid this year came to an end with a disastrous television spot directed by Francis Ford Coppola, Brown still holds some sway over the party. His support for tax cuts, a defense build-up, and harsh immigration restrictions would represent a hard pivot to the right for Carter, if Brown is selected.

Of course, Brown's roots in California could open up the Golden State as a key battleground. It is currently thought to be non-competitive because of Reagan's popularity there, but perhaps Brown's oddball nature could win them over to the Democratic camp?

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Ed Muskie is Secretary of State and a former presidential candidate. In 1976, Muskie was strongly considered as Carter's running mate, so it is not entirely surprising that the president is ruminating on selecting him four years later. The Secretary has certainly received bipartisan plaudits for his handling of the Iranian hostage crisis and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan

Of course, if Muskie were to be selected, he would be forced to resign and would face withering partisan criticism over whether his couple months at Foggy Bottom were just a stunt to raise his profile after his disastrous presidential bid in 1972.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Pat Lucey is the U.S. Ambassador to Mexico and a popular former Governor of Wisconsin. A registered Democrat, Lucey endorsed Ted Kennedy's bid against Jimmy Carter this year. A Catholic from a must-win state for the Carter campaign, Lucey's selection would strengthen Anderson's hold on disaffected liberal Democrats, but risk the "spoiler" issue becoming a major theme.

Then again, surveys indicate Lucey's star has fallen inside the state of Wisconsin due to his liberal policies, so there are some questions over just how much appeal he really has to Democrats.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Barbara Jordan is a former Democratic Congresswoman from Texas. Best known for her stirring keynote address at the 1976 DNC and her opening remarks during the Watergate impeachment hearings, Jordan is a liberal icon, even if her actual political beliefs are closer to the center.

Jordan was forced to step down from Congress in 1978 due to declining health, which could become an issue were she to be selected as Anderson's running mate. Additionally, she is a lesbian.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Walter Cronkite is the most trusted man in America. He has served as lead anchorman for CBS Evening News since 1962, and has reported on events such as the Kennedy assassination, the Vietnam War, the Apollo 11 Moon mission, and most recently, the hostage crisis in Iran.

On paper, Cronkite seems like a golden ticket for the Anderson campaign. Even stranger, Cronkite is reportedly ecstatic about the possibility of being considered, and would agree to join the ticket in a heartbeat. But some of the iconic anchorman's own views hardly represent the middle Americans his broadcasts appeal to most.

fields.description: Candidate description here.

Grandson of President William Henry Harrison, Benjamin Harrison seems almost pre-ordained to become President. The refusal of James G. Blaine to seek the nomination at the Republican National Convention has resulted in Harrison's nomination on the eighth ballot.

A key advantage he has in the upcoming campaign is that he is running against Grover Cleveland. A key shortcoming, however, is also that he is running against Grover Cleveland. This election is dominated by the tariff issue, and the ethnic vote will be hotly contested as a result.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1888 election!

Well done! Cleveland was a strong opponent, but you have ran a fantastic campaign over the past several months. You have proven to the nation that the election of 1884 was a fluke, and that the Republican Party is still the natural party of governance. Now it's up to you to restore a sensible tariff policy, and maybe even pursue the limited coinage of silver.

Should you perform anywhere near as well during your Presidency as you have over the past four months, you should be in prime position to win a second term and cement yourself in the history books. Will the Silver Democrats take control now that Cleveland is out of the picture? Who knows? Whatever happens, best of luck!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1888 election.

Some thought Cleveland to be vulnerable, but he was a skilled opponent, and it was simply not to be this time. He has proven that his 1884 victory was more than a fluke — it was a real mandate for lasting Democratic leadership.

So where does this leave you? It's hard to say. You put up a strong showing, and you remain popular within the Republican Party, so it's entirely possible that you could make another go at it sometime in the future. But that's not guaranteed. It's not even guaranteed that the same faction of the Republican Party will be in power in 1892, after two successive losses. Whatever you do end up doing, good luck!

fields.description:
There are times when Grover Cleveland seems like a one-man army. In 1884, he upset the postbellum order, seizing the presidency as a reformist and a Bourbon Democrat. He has achieved mixed results. His liberal use of the veto, especially for Civil War pensions and the Texas Seed Bill, has frustrated some. Elsewhere, he is a committed sound money man and a foreign policy non-interventionist.

The issue dominating this election is tariff policy. Cleveland is an aggressive opponent of tariffs, dedicating his December 1887 State of the Union written address entirely to tariff reform. This comes with upsides and downsides, especially considering the ethnic dimension of this issue.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1888 election!

Most impressive! It was a little iffy there for a bit, but you have pulled through to become the first two-term Democrat since Andrew Jackson. You have proven to the nation that your 1884 victory was more than just a fluke — it was a real mandate for lasting Democratic leadership.

What's on the plate for your second term? Hopefully you can keep a lid on the Congress's wasteful spending, and continue your crusade for lower tariffs. If all goes well, you can pass the torch to another Bourbon Democrat in 1892 — although it probably won't be poor Allen Thurman. But for now, forget all that. Sit back in the White House with Frances and relax. You've earned it.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry, you have lost the 1888 election.

This comes as a surprise to few. Harrison was a strong candidate, and his campaign was expertly managed. It seems like your fluke victory in 1884 was just that — a fluke. Harrison will no doubt try to hike up those tariffs, and maybe even pursue a bimetallist monetary policy.

So where does this leave you? It's hard to say. At 51 years old, you are the youngest ex-president in American history. You settle nicely into private life and prepare to start a family. But unbeknownst to you, as you prepare to leave the White House for the last time, your wife Frances tells a servant, “We are coming back just four years from today.”

fields.description: Prohibition candidate. His views aren't mainstream. Yet.
n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Levi P. Morton is a former Congressman and ambassador to France. He declined overtures from James Garfield to serve as his running mate in 1880 on the advice of political ally Roscoe Conkling. This time, he is willing to accept the position. He is supported by Stalwart Tom Platt and the rest of the New York delegation.

He could come in handy in New York, the largest state in the Union. Harrison's electoral math becomes very difficult without New York in his column.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
William Walter Phelps is a Congressman from New Jersey, and the preferred choice of James G. Blaine. However, the New York delegation is flatly refusing to consider him.

If Harrison cared strongly about it, he could probably intervene on Phelps' behalf and weasel him onto the ticket. He may come in handy in New Jersey, another major swing state, although that is not nearly as crucial as New York.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
In 1885, Vice President Thomas Hendricks died in office. Since there is no procedure to fill a vacancy in the Vice Presidency (yet), the office has remained empty since then. This vacancy could be potentially filled by Allen Thurman.

On one hand, Thurman is a true old school Democrat, and could help placate those skeptical of Cleveland's liberalism. His extensive history of elected office in Ohio also may come in handy, since Ohio is a crucial swing state in any election. On the other hand, he is a retired, elderly politician who may be unable to campaign very aggressively or dynamically.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Another possibility for Vice President is Isaac P. Gray. Not only was he a Union cavalry commander in the Civil War, but he even pushed the hated postwar amendments through the Indiana Senate as a state senator. He switched to the Democratic Party in 1876 over the Grant administration's rampant corruption. He has since had a career in Democratic politics, serving as Governor of Indiana.

There is a chance that his selection might not go over well with the convention because of his past actions as a Republican. However, he could make for an unorthodox presence on the campaign trail, and maybe even woo disaffected Republicans away from Harrison. Picking him would basically be a giant gamble.

fields.description:
Jackson has been the frontrunner for the presidency since his controversial loss in the 1824 election – a result he and his partisans blame on a corrupt bargain between Adams and fourth-place nominee Henry Clay. His position as a man of the people appeals most strongly to the South and West.

Jackson’s military career will be a double-edged sword during the campaign. His heroism in the War of 1812 cannot be denied, but neither can his ferocious temper and savagery towards Native Americans. The Adams campaign will waste no time branding him an unsophisticated brute.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1828 election.

Your election had been practically assured by the lethargy of Adams' forces, but this is still a tremendous victory.

You have thus far kept your priorities close to your chest, but the issues of nullification and the frontier will soon be on your docket. For now, though, content yourself with a raucous party at the Executive Mansion and hope that the era of political mudslinging is now through.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1828 election.

What? Adams had been counted out since you were first nominated three years ago. In the interim, a series of blunders by your campaign has contributed to a colossal upset.

Adams and his puppetmaster, Henry Clay, will likely take this victory as a mandate for the American System and a return to the Era of Good Feelings. The president will likely be resisted in his attempts to bring an end to partisanship by your allies Calhoun and Van Buren. As for you, your poor health likely means a permanent return to the Hermitage.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow. No candidate has achieved a majority in the Electoral College!

This is a most unusual situation. The administration's supporters have outperformed in the congressional elections, meaning his election is prohibitively likely, but your supporters are determined to stop history from repeating itself. No matter what happens, this does not bode well for the future of democracy.

fields.description:
Adams seeks re-election after winning the presidency in an 1825 contingent election. His appointment of runner-up Henry Clay as Secretary of State and failure to enact his domestic program gave way to allegations of cronyism and weakness that have dogged him for his entire term.

Adams boasts a long resume and perhaps the most fearsome intellect in America, but his reputation seems to be hurting him more than anything else this year. The president’s previous support of the Federalist Party and famous last name help him in New England, but his perceived elitism will do him little good in Western battlegrounds.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1828 election.

Not even you expected this outcome. Your allies have gained in Congress, and Jackson's are stunned into submission, meaning you will have plenty of leverage to pass Clay's ambitious domestic program into law.

You, however, are more interested in eliminating the scourge of partisanship from public life. Good luck restoring the honor of the office over the next four years!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry. You have lost the 1828 election

This was the result most Americans expected. Jackson has swept you out of Washington, and promises to uproot the American System.

Distraught though you are, you are looking forward to the prospect of a lengthy retirement. A biography of your father is a particular passion project that is likely to come out of this defeat, so long as you resist the temptation to re-enter public life.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow. No candidate has achieved a majority in the Electoral College

This is a most unusual situation. The administration's supporters have outperformed in the congressional elections, meaning your election is prohibitively likely, but Jackson's supporters are determined to stop history from repeating itself. No matter what happens, this does not bode well for the future of democracy.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
John Calhoun is the incumbent vice president, elected by a landslide margin in the electoral college four years ago while the House bickered over the next president. Expecting Jackson to retire after one term, he has already agreed to join forces in hopes of advancing his own presidential ambitions.

A staunch nationalist in the Monroe cabinet, Calhoun has since rejected the American System and become a fierce critic of protective tariffs, a change of view that will limit his appeal outside of the Deep South. Nonetheless, he is the preferred candidate of Martin Van Buren.

With John Calhoun joining the opposition effort and Henry Clay refusing the president’s advances, Treasury Secretary Richard Rush is the only member of the cabinet willing to join the Adams party’s ticket.

Rush is a Pennsylvanian, but the difference he’ll make in that state is negligible at best. A ticket of two Northerners is considered tantamount to political suicide, but Adams appears to have little interest in winning the election anyway.

fields.description:
Lyndon Baines Johnson has been President of the United States since that tragic afternoon in Dallas, 1963. In the months since then, LBJ has hit the ground running on issues ranging from tax reform to civil rights as his Great Society comes to fruition.

However, not all is well in America. Disorder in the streets, disillusionment about the status-quo, and a ballooning problem in Vietnam has given President Johnson issues, even inside his own party. Still, with Republicans poised to nominate the unorthodox, controversial, and ultra-conservative Barry Goldwater, Johnson remains a heavyweight favorite this election year.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2016 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Donald Trump, you have become the first woman elected to serve as President.

On the political front, it is unclear how much of your agenda you will be able to push forward with the current Congress. Hopefully your victory has helped Democrats further down the ballot. Start packing and prepare to move back into the White House!
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

Many of your supporters are despondent that you have faltered to the likes of Donald Trump. Many in the left wing of the party are furious that you pushed their candidate aside, only to lose. Time will tell how Trump operates as President. As for you, a long and sometimes ambiguous political career seems to be coming to its end.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

No candidate secured a majority in the Electoral College. However, the Republicans won a majority in Congress and will elevate Trump to the Presidency. Time will tell how things go in that regard. As for you, a long and sometimes ambiguous political career seems to be coming to its end.

fields.description:
Barry Morris Goldwater is a prototypical son of the West and the reluctant Republican nominee for President in 1964. His rugged individualism, John Wayne-esque image, and capital-C Conservatism help cultivate a careful facade which has allowed Goldwater to overrun the GOP establishment during his party's primary.

Senator Goldwater is the evident underdog against Johnson, and his unwaveringly blunt statements on issues from Vietnam to civil rights have not helped his case, especially with other Republican stars like Rockefeller and Romney not yet supporting his campaign. Still, Goldwater has a loyal army and a growing movement. He only hopes to avoid total embarrassment in November.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 2016 election.

In spite of a hard-fought challenge from Hillary Clinton, you have shocked the world with your election victory.

On the political front, you have the bully pulpit in your favor, but support in Congress in uncertain. Will you govern as a more traditional conservative, or will you make a break from orthodoxy?
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 2016 election.

Many of your supporters are despondent that you have faltered to the likes of Hillary Clinton. Republicans in general believe this was a very winnable election, and are enraged that you came in to blow it. Luckily, there are any number of ways for you to take advantage of your newfound exposure. One rumor even has you founding a television station to profit from the aggrieved sensibilities of your followers. The future is in your hands.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! You have pulled out 2016 election.

No candidate secured a majority in the Electoral College. However, the Republicans won a majority in Congress and will elevate you to the Presidency. Time will tell how things go in that regard. Any mutual affection between you and Congress is predicted to be short-lived, but you've pulled off a number of surprises to get this far.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
William Edward Miller is a New York Congressman and the current Chairman of the Republican National Committee. A loyal conservative who happens to hail from Goldwater's enemy territory on the Eastern seaboard, party strategists believe that Miller's geographic balance and Catholic background will make him an adequate running-mate.

Of course, Congressman Miller has zero name recognition on the national scene, and most believe he would only be poached for the ticket as Goldwater's friend, or as the last possible choice should everyone else refuse.

Gerald R. Ford Jr. is the ever-reliable Congressman from Michigan's fifth, and the Chairman of the House Republican Conference. Ford is a consistent conservative who nonetheless has maintained strong ties with colleagues across the political spectrum, including Michigan governor George Romney, who is still holding out against Goldwater.

A college football star, Ford would certainly add a sorely needed new energy to the GOP ticket that may amount to a second wind for the nominee. Unfortunately, Ford has low name recognition, and he is hesitant to put his career on the line for Barry Goldwater.

Dr. Walter Judd is the esteemed, and recently defeated, Republican Congressman from Minnesota's fifth district, who is many of the campaign staff's top choice for the position of running-mate. As conservative as he is consistent, Judd has been at the forefront of America's battle against communism since his time in Nationalist China as a young man, and he would hopefully ease fears that Goldwater is trigger happy.

Congressman Judd is a great favorite of General Eisenhower, still bitter about the nominating process, and his nomination would likely help bring together a divided party who barely stand a chance against President Johnson when united.

James Allen Rhodes is the recently elected Governor of Ohio, and a late Goldwater backer at the Republican National Convention. Winning his 1962 campaign against an incumbent in a landslide, many feel that Rhodes could be key in holding Ohio, a state that no Republican candidate for President has won without.

Governor Rhodes, despite his support for the Senator from Arizona at the convention, is reluctant to join what many consider a doomed ticket, especially as he seems to have high ambitions in his own right. His grounded approach to creating jobs and building infrastructure could help cool a campaign that finds itself dealing with matters of life and death more and more by the day.

Hubert Horatio Humphrey is a United States Senator from Minnesota and the preeminent liberal in America today. There are few politicians outside party leadership or the federal government with name recognition like Hubert Humphrey, with crowds cheering for every mention of his brave stand for civil rights at the 1948 Democratic convention, almost any group has strong feelings one way or the other for the "Happy Warrior."

Humphrey has been the expected pick since Johnson first began making calls about his re-election in the days after Kennedy's assassination, and the Senator has more than put in the work for LBJ on the Civil Rights Act to justify his nomination for the President's old job.

Eugene Joseph McCarthy is the other Senator from Minnesota, and most certainly the least known of President Johnson's shortlist of running-mates. A quiet, dry, sagely Catholic who is better accustomed to poetry than the drinking and gambling of the President's clique, McCarthy has nonetheless made himself a useful foot soldier for Lyndon Johnson since entering the Senate in 1958. Four years ago, he gained fame by speaking for Stevenson at the 1960 Democratic convention.

Senator McCarthy is about as liberal as his senior colleague from Minnesota, but far softer spoken and dull in his execution of said beliefs. Many Southerners, including John Connally, view McCarthy as a favorable alternative to Hubert Humphrey, and Gene himself seems to believe he'll be getting the nod.

Edmund G. Brown Sr. is the incumbent Governor of California since 1959, the first since Franklin Roosevelt was in office. Fresh off his thumping win against Richard Nixon during the midterm elections, Brown is expected to have great sway over the happenings at the 1964 Democratic National Convention.

Brown is a bona fide liberal who has, to his own benefit and more often misfortune, taken brave stances on infrastructure, education, civil rights, and the death penalty to name only a few issues. In some respects, it is said that he has done in California what Johnson seeks to do nationally with the Great Society. Electorally, California is a hotbed for right wing activity, and some worry Goldwater may stand a chance there if Pat Brown isn't on the ticket.

Robert Strange McNamara is the incumbent Secretary of Defense and, according to some, President Lyndon Johnson's personal choice for his running-mate. The Kennedy clan's eminent Republican ally has been tasked with running America's war machine as global tensions continue to shoot through the roof.

With the lingering failure of the Bay of Pigs, the growing conflict in Vietnam, and Barry Goldwater's candidacy, it is believed that McNamara could add further credibility to the President's ticket on foreign affairs. Others fear that he simply doesn't have what it takes to survive in politics.

fields.description:
Ulysses S. Grant was elected in 1868 in an election defined by questions of reconstruction. Over his first term, Grant has fought fiercely to maintain federal protections for Black voters and to dismantle redeemer organizations like the Ku Klux. Yet his work on this front has been repeatedly waylaid by other issues, from an ill-considered plan to purchase Santo Domingo to a string of corruption scandals from within his administration.

Now, Grant faces a loose coalition of frustrated former allies and ancient foes. Grant is held in high esteem by most, and he feels comfortable to run a traditional campaign while relying on the Republican machine. But the Liberal break does pose a real threat, and Grant must ask himself how much compromise he is willing to accept to secure re-election.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1896 election.

In spite of a real scare from Mr. Bryan, you have done your part to preserve good order in the United States.

None of that changes the fact that the country is facing a depression with millions out of work. Are you the man to lead the nation back into greatness?

Your first order of business will be tariff increases to stimulate industry, as well as a new commitment to the gold standard.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Sorry! You have lost the 1896 election.

The titans of American industry were counting on you to put down this nonsense idea of free silver, and to protect them from the other whims of the populist Democrats. Your defeat will go down as one of the most ignominous in the history of American politics.

Bryan's victory stings all the more because after the inept Cleveland Administration, this election shouldn't have been close. Needless to say, your political career is over.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Wow! You have won a true nail-biter.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, marking the first time this has happened since 1824. Fortunately for you, the majority of U.S. states have Republican controlled congressional delegations, and they will cast their votes for you accordingly.

The important thing is that you won. Go about implementing your agenda accordingly, and pay no attention to Democrats and agitators who call for 'compromise' and 'conciliation'.

fields.description:
Horace Greeley is the long-time owner of the New York Tribune, famous for his utopian patriotism through his nationally circulated editorials. Once a loyal Republican, Greeley has grown enamoured with a dream of reuniting North and South, credulously backing southern leaders who claim to have accepted civil rights. After years of enmity with Grant, Greeley has used his political savvy to take control of a reformist Republican splinter party expected to lead the charge against Grant this election.

Democrats and Liberals have accepted that Greeley's run is unavoidable, but many rue their choice of candidate. Greeley still holds many Republican beliefs, including a disinterest in reform of tariff or civil service, and his long record of eccentric causes may also prove easy fodder for attack. Yet some Republicans still worry. If Greeley can reassure his base and make good use of Republican strife, he may still have a shot at victory.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1896 election.

"The Great Commoner" will soon be President of the United States! Nobody with your political views has ever sniffed the Presidency, let alone won it, and with that in mind your supporters are rioting frenziedly in the streets. The sweetest speech of all will be your victory speech tomorrow in Lincoln, Nebraska. Prepare to enact your reform agenda and most importantly the free coinage of silver.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Farewell. You have lost the 1872 election.

Alas, it seems you were unable to overcome your scandals and President Grant's great popularity. You will pass on shortly after the election in the grip of grief, leaving your electoral votes scattered among a handful of candidates. Despite the many attacks you endured from Grant's allies, your death will cause many Republicans to mourn. You will be remembered as an eccentric abolishist, your last days forgotten.

Reconstruction and disorder will continue under Grant, though economic hardships and flagging northern interest will see it draw to a close in time. The reform movement you hijacked will live on in both parties, as Liberal Republicans return to Grant or join with the Democrats. Most of them will die believing your nomination is what led their party to run.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
Sorry! You have lost in a squeaker.

No candidate achieved a majority of the electoral votes, marking the first time this has happened since 1824. Unfortunately for you, the majority of U.S. states have Republican controlled congressional delegations, and they will cast their votes for William McKinley.

Given the incredibly close nature of the election, you can certainly set your sights on a political comeback in 1900, if that is what you desire.

fields.description: Hey, did you know this guy actually was senior counsel for Jefferson Davis? and Greeley paid for his bond, too. So everyone here except Grant really liked Jeff D is my point.
n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Henry Wilson is the junior senator from Massachusetts. Beginning as an orphan and later a shoe maker, Wilson rose from poverty to become a Whig, and later, one of the Republican Party's first senators. A radical through his career, Wilson initially was pushed as a possible running mate in 1868, but was ultimately passed over for Schuyler Colfax. Now, many hope to see him reconsidered.

Wilson has many supporters across the country. He is a Radical, an able campaigner, a loyalist to Grant's agenda, and will help hold New England after Sumner's many denunciations of the President. In a party increasingly dominated by rings and bosses, Wilson's nomination will reassure workers that Grant remains a man of the people.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Schuyler Colfax is the current Vice President of the United States. As Speaker of the House for much of the civil war, Colfax fought hard for the passage of the thirteenth and fourteenth amendments. Though a radical who fought against President Johnson, Colfax's initial selection over Benjamin Wade was in line with the goals of the 1868 convention - casting congressional reconstruction in a moderate light.

In the wake of the Liberal breakaway, this moderation has become a fright to many Radicals. Rumors abound that Colfax's true feelings lie with the turncoats, and he himself has been reluctant to accept a second term. President Grant's primary concern is sectional - as a fellow midwesterner, Colfax may bring less to the ticket than a Vice President from a different region.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
Benjamin Gratz Brown is the current governor of Missouri. A rare electoral winner among the Liberal Republicans, he and long-time rival Carl Schurz are the twin founders of the Liberal Republican movement both in Missouri and across the nation. During the Cincinnati convention, it was Benjamin Gratz Brown's unexpected endorsement which allowed for Greeley's nomination.

Brown's importance to the Liberals make him an obvious choice for a campaign in need of legitimacy, and he has a long-standing appeal to the electorally crucial German minority. Yet his rivalry with Schurz has left him as controversial as Greeley himself, and his rumored abuse of alcohol may jeopardize Greeley's upstanding reputation.

fields.description: n/a
fields.description_as_running_mate:
George Washington Julian is a former congressman from Indiana. His career is typical of Liberal Republican leadership; after spending decades as an unabashed radical -- including a previous vice presidential campaign under the Free Soil Party -- Julian was forced out by Oliver Morton's state machine and moderated on amnesty shortly after.

Julian provides a satisfying alternative to the controversial B. Gratz Brown, a proper Liberal Republican from a key state willing to stand on your ticket. His time in Congress also proves a sincere commitment to land and tariff reform. Yet that same commitment drove Greeley to oppose his renomination in 1868, and places the two at a distance now. Even beyond this, it remains to be seen if the South can accept a vice president who once called for Lee and Davis to hang.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
Cassius Clay is a founding hero to the Republican Party. Born to a famous family of southern slaveholders, Clay chose instead to fight for abolition, publishing an anti-slavery newspaper and later founding the Republican Party in Kentucky. In 1860, he nearly became Lincoln's vice president - instead, he supported Lincoln as a diplomat and soldier. Yet as radicalism swept the nation, Clay found himself increasingly out of step. Clay now sees himself as fighting despotism by advocating 'universal amnesty'.

Though Clay is a towering figure, his nomination would cause much uproar. Clay is a Greeleyite and a protectionist, and his nomination would only further alienate those slighted by the events in Cincinnati. But like Greeley, Clay is committed above all else to winning over Southern hearts.

fields.description:
Grover Cleveland is the newly-elected Governor of New York and former mayor of Buffalo. A committed reformer and enemy of Tammany Hall, he has made a name for himself after being elected governor of the largest state in the country by historic margins. Other than reform, Cleveland proves himself to be neutral on all the other dangerous issues, with no record of rebellion, no embarrassments from Reconstruction, and no thoughts on tariffs. Eight years after the hotly-contested 1876 election, Democrats need a candidate they know can win, and with Tilden out of the picture, Cleveland is that man.

Cleveland will have to unite the Democratic Party around his candidacy, and appeal to disaffected Independent Republicans, third-party voters, and ethnic Irish and Germans to be able to win.
fields.electoral_victory_message:
Congratulations! You have won the 1884 Presidential Election.

Fate has landed you in the White House, Governor Cleveland. As you prepare to resign the office of Governor of New York, flipping through the thousands of letters and telegraphs of congratulations, you think upon all that has brought you here. Perhaps it was Burchard's remarks, your personal integrity, or Blaine's own scandals. Either way, you are glad that this mud-slinging campaign is over. It has been a terrible one, for sure.

To your friends, Harold Frederic and Shan Bissell, you write: Imagine a man standing in my place, with positively no ambition for a higher position than I now hold, and in constant apprehension that he may be called upon to assume burdens and duties the greatest and highest that a human being can take upon himself. I can not look upon the prospect of success in this campaign with any joy, but only with a very serious kind of awe. Is this right? I look upon the four years next to come as a dreadful self-inflicted penance for the good of my country. I can see no pleasure in it and no satisfaction, only a hope that I may be of service to my people.
fields.electoral_loss_message:
Unfortunately, you have lost the 1884 Presidential Election.

Even with the Mugwump revolt and the various trappings of the Blaine campaign in scandal, you have lost the election - perhaps the closest since 1876. Democrats cry out at election fraud, just like they did with Tilden, but you have already consigned yourself to the Governor's Mansion. Was it Halpin? Was it your other scandals? Either way, the nation has proved that it is not in the mood for your reforms, or your candidacy.

You will soon return, hopefully with some vigor, to your position as Governor of New York. The Mugwumps are disappointed, and will probably return to try and nominate Edmunds in four years' time. You are still a major political player, though - there is no telling if you cannot enter into the running again in 1888, though you will most likely again face the ire of Tammany. For now, though, the Democrats are once again denied of the White House.
fields.no_electoral_majority_message:
The 1884 Presidential Election resulted in... A Tie!

It appears as if, draped in the mantle of Tilden, you have done what he was able to do - force the Republicans into an uneasy spot. You have tied in electoral votes, that much is for sure. Democrat and Republican alike cry fraud, and perhaps that will decide the true winner of the election.

For now, you have at least reclaimed the standing of the Democratic Party as a party able to compete nationally. You might want to extract concessions from Blaine in order to confirm him as the winner, just like Tilden did in 1876, and return to your role as New York Governor. Or, you could whip your support amongst the Mugwumps to put you at the helm of the United States. Whatever you do, the next four years will be fiery and dramatic.

fields.description:
James G. Blaine is President Arthur's former Secretary of State and a former Senator from Maine. Having contested the nomination in 1876 and 1880, the Plumed Knight is the leader of the Half-Breed faction of the Republican Party. Blaine has a magnetic and frank disposition, but his public record is dirtied with scandals and allegations of corruption.

Despite originally preferring General William Tecumseh Sherman, Blaine emerged as the front-runner at the convention and his momentum has carried him to the nomination. He faces a Republican Party divided into factions - Half-Breeds, Stalwarts, Independents, and ultra-reformist Mugwumps. To win the election, Blaine needs to keep the race focused on the issues and deflect from his scandalous reputation.

fields.description_as_running_mate:
Thomas Andrews Hendricks is the courtly former running mate of Samuel Tilden and former Governor of Indiana. Democratic papers have spoken of a revival of the old ticket that almost brought Democrats the presidency, but with Tilden unavailable this year due to his health, Hendricks represents a revival of the old ticket with Tilden, while also serving as a bridge to Tammany Hall's Honest John Kelly, a personal friend of his.

If Cleveland were to pick Hendricks as his running mate, it would be the beginning of a fence-mending measure within the Democratic Party, attempting to bring back both anti-Cleveland forces at the convention and Tammany Hall. Draped in Tilden's mantle, Cleveland would represent the Old Ticket, but with a boy taking his place

Henry Gassaway Davis is a former Senator from West Virginia. A high-tariff man and staunch protectionist, Davis is a large landowner and coal baron whose banked funds and moneyed hands might assist Cleveland in winning the election.

Davis's high-tariff opinions are, however, in opposition with much of the Democratic Party, and he has many connections to Blaine - Blaine is Davis's personal friend, and his campaign manager, Steven Elkins, is his son-in-law. If Cleveland were to pick Davis, he would forego much of the Democratic base while securing much-needed funds for the campaign.

John Alexander Black Jack Logan is a Senator from Illinois and former general in the Civil War. Originally a Democrat, Logan made a name for himself as a Union war hero in the Civil War. He defected to the Republican Party, becoming one of the most respected Radical Republicans in Congress. Logan is a ferocious attack-dog, too, willing to wave the bloody shirt. He is supported by former President Grant as well as Black Republicans as the most outspoken Republican on civil rights this year.

Despite his impeccable record as a war hero, Logan is a poor orator with shifting views on finance, government, and civil service reform. Logan was also a member of the Stalwart wing of the party, contrasting with Blaine's Half-Breed leadership. As Blaine's running mate, the Black Eagle would present an alternative to Blaine's focus on the issues.

John Sherman is a sitting Senator from Ohio and the brother of famed Union General William Tecumseh Sherman. With a clean slate on temperance and prohibition, Sherman can be counted on by Blaine to carry his home state. Sherman has a talent for administration, and is friends with the business community and supported by Black voters.

Sherman was one of the main opponents to Blaine for the nomination in 1884, and has promised to deliver Ohio, a crucial state, to Blaine. His name also serves as a way to wave the bloody shirt, due to his connection with his older brother. His high-tariff stance, however, might weaken the Republican ticket in states where the tariff is unpopular.

Robert Todd Lincoln is the eldest son of President Abraham Lincoln and the current United States Secretary of War. His name carries all the prestige that Blaine needs to carry the nation - the ticket would elect itself. He is cold, unimaginative, and reserved, however, and there are questions surrounding his personality, especially about him putting his own mother in an asylum.

More than that, though, Lincoln has stated that he does not want to run as vice presidential nominee, and his general disaffection for the presidential race and possibility to bring personal scandal into the election might hurt Blaine's chances. It would take a mountain for Blaine to move to get Lincoln on his ticket.

fields.description:
Stoic. Methodical. Restrained. George Washington treats himself as a figure of singular historical importance and, in the eyes of Federalists, he is. His leadership during the Revolutionary War has been built by others into a thing of legends. His tight control over his emotions has allowed him to appear like a creature of inhuman modesty. Even in his old age, Washington appears large, forceful, and imposing—exactly the strong leader that a young Nation needs.

Washington is also one of the wealthiest men in the Republic. He owes his money to his inheritance of a vast slave plantation and the theft, sale, and aggressive speculation of Native lands. His vast fortune is now jeopardized by the Nation’s political instability and deteriorating economy. He desires a powerful federal government to help recoup his investments.
